Fragesätze

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Fragesätze" in German are question sentences that are used to ask questions. These sentences are formed differently from normal declarative sentences and usually start with a question word or a question particle.

2. Usage

- Here are some details about forming and using "Fragesätze" in German:

1. Question words

- Question words are used to ask questions about specific information, such as who, what, when, where, why, and how. In German, these words are "wer" (who), "was" (what), "wann" (when), "wo" (where), "warum" (why), and "wie" (how). They are typically placed at the beginning of the sentence, followed by the verb and the subject.

Examples:

  • Wer ist das? 
    (Who is that?)
  • Was machst du heute? 
    (What are you doing today?)
  • Wann kommst du zurück? 
    (When are you coming back?)
  • Wo wohnst du? 
    (Where do you live?)
  • Warum hast du das gemacht? 
    (Why did you do that?)
  • Wie geht es dir? 
    (How are you?)
2. Question particles

- Question particles are used to turn declarative sentences into questions. The most common question particle in German is "ob" (whether/if), which is used to ask yes/no questions. The particle is placed at the beginning of the sentence, followed by the subject and verb.

Examples:

  • Ob du kommst? 
    (Are you coming?)
  • Ob es heute regnen wird? 
    (Will it rain today?)
3. Inverted word order

- In German, the word order in a question sentence is inverted from the normal declarative word order. The verb usually comes first, followed by the subject.

Examples:

  • Hast du das Buch gelesen? 
    (Have you read the book?)
  • Kannst du mir helfen? 
    (Can you help me?)
  • Möchtest du einen Kaffee? 
    (Would you like a coffee?)
4. Modal verbs

- When asking a question with a modal verb (such as "können", "müssen", or "wollen"), the modal verb is placed first, followed by the subject and the infinitive of the main verb.

Examples:

  • Kannst du mir helfen? 
    (Can you help me?)
  • Müssen wir das machen? 
    (Do we have to do that?)
  • Wollen wir ins Kino gehen? 
    (Do we want to go to the cinema?)

- In summary, "Fragesätze" in German are question sentences that are formed using question words, question particles, inverted word order, and modal verbs. They are used to ask questions and gather specific information from the listener.

Separable and Inseparable Verbs in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. List of Separable Verbs
  3. List of Inseparable Verbs
  4. German Verbs that are Separable or Inseparable

1. Introduction

- Separable verbs (Trennbare Verben) and inseparable verbs (Untrennbare Verben) in German are verbs whose meaning is altered by the addition of a prefix. Prefixes that are separable are separated from their verb in the conjugated form e.g. anstehen - ich stehe an (to queue - I queue). Whereas, inseparable prefixes cannot be separated from their verb e.g. bestehen - du bestehst (to pass - you pass). The prefix determines whether a verb is separable or not.

2. List of Separable Verbs

- The verbs with the following prefixes are separable:

ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, bei-, ein-, los-, mit-, nach-, her-, hin-, vor-, weg-, zu-, zurück-

In the finite form

- These verbs are separated from their prefix, which usually comes at the end of the sentence.

Examples:

  • Ich stehe an der Kasse an
In the past participle

- We add ge- between the prefix and the verb.

Examples:

  • Ich habe an der Kasse angestanden.

3. List of Inseparable Verbs

- Verbs with the following prefixes are inseparable:

be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-

These prefixes remain a permanent part of the verb, even in the finite form.

Examples:

  • Ich bestehe die Prüfung.
The the past participle of inseparable verbs is not formed with ge.

Examples:

  • Ich habe die Prüfung bestanden

4. German Verbs that are Separable or Inseparable

- The verbs with the following prefixes can be either separable or inseparable:

durch-, hinter-, über-, um-, unter-

Some verbs with these prefixes are always separable.

Examples: umschauen

  • er schaut sich um
Some other verbs with these prefixes are never separable.

Examples: umarmen

  • sie umarmt ihn
Some verbs with these prefixes can be either separable or inseparable

- In this case, the separable verb and the inseparable verb have two different meanings.

Examples: umfahren

  • Er fährt das Schild um.
  • Er umfährt das Schild.

1. Accusative Case - Declension of Nouns

1. Introduction

- The accusative case, also called the accusative object or direct object, is used for the thing or person receiving the direct action of a verb. Because word order is freer in German grammar, we use the accusative case to mark the direct object in a sentence by changing the article of masculine nouns and adding -n/-en to some nouns. The accusative case follows certain verbs and prepositions. We can use the questions wen (whom) or was (what) to find the direct object.

Examples:

  • Der Junge hat eine Freundin. Er spielt sehr gut Gitarre und hat ein Liebeslied für die Freundin komponiert.
  • Er singt der Freundin das Lied vor.
2. Usage

- We use nouns in the accusative case:

1. After certain verbs (accusative object): haben, singen, spielen, komponieren, …

Examples:

  • Der Junge hat eine Freundin.
  • Er spielt Gitarre.
  • Er hat ein Liebeslied komponiert.
  • Er singt das Lied.
2. After certain prepositions: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um

Examples:

  • Er hat ein Liebeslied für die Freundin komponiert.
3. As the direct object in sentences with more than one object

Examples:

  • Er singt der Freundin das Lied vor.

- Some masculine nouns have the endings -n or -en in the accusative, dative and genitive.

  • masculine noun ending in ent: der Assistent - den Assistenten
  • others, e.g: der Herr - den Herrn, der Mensch - den Menschen

2. Accusative Case - Declension of Pronouns

1. Introduction

- The accusative case, also the accusative object or direct object, follows certain verbs and prepositions. It is used for the thing or person receiving the direct action of a verb. Because word order is freer in German grammar, we use the accusative case to mark the direct object in a sentence by using different personal pronouns and changing the ending of masculine possessive pronouns. We can use the questions wen/was to find out whom/what is recieving the action of the verb.

Examples:

  • Karin sucht ihren Hut. Ohne ihn will sie nicht aus dem Haus gehen.
  • Sie hat nur den Hut ihres Vaters gefunden, nicht ihren. Jemand muss ihn ihr weggenommen haben.
2. Usage

- We use pronouns in the accustive case:

1. after certain verbs (accusative object), e. g. suchen, finden, …

Examples:

  • Karin sucht ihren Hut.
  • Sie hat nur den Hut ihres Vaters gefunden, nicht ihren.
2. after certain prepositions e.g. durch, für, gegen, ohne, um

Examples:

  • Ohne ihn will sie nicht aus dem Haus gehen.
3. as the direct object in sentences with more than one object

Examples:

  • Jemand muss ihn ihr weggenommen haben.

To note:

- If a pronoun is the direct object, then it is placed before the indirect object in a sentence.

Examples:

  • Jemand muss Karin den Hut weggenommen haben.
  • Jemand muss ihr den Hut weggenommen haben.
  • Jemand muss ihn Karin weggenommen haben.
  • Jemand muss ihn ihr weggenommen haben.

Andere

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Andere" in German means "others" or "other ones". It is a pronoun that can be used in various ways depending on the context.

2. Usage

- Here are some common uses of "Andere" in German:

1. As a pronoun

- As a pronoun, "andere" can refer to people or things that are different from the one(s) already mentioned. It is often used in phrases like "einige andere" (some others), "viele andere" (many others), or "die anderen" (the others).

Examples:

  • "Ich habe gestern ein Buch gekauft, aber ich will heute andere Bücher kaufen."
    (Yesterday, I bought a book, but today I want to buy other books.)
  • "Er ist nicht wie die anderen Jungs in der Klasse."
    (He is not like the other boys in the class.)
2. As an adjective

- As an adjective, "andere" describes something that is different or distinct from something else. It can be used with or without an article, depending on the context.

Examples:

  • "Es gibt andere Möglichkeiten, dieses Problem zu lösen."
    (There are other ways to solve this problem.)
  • "Ich habe ein anderes Auto gekauft."
    (I bought a different car.)
3. As an adverb

- As an adverb, "andere" modifies a verb or adjective to indicate a difference or change. It is often used with verbs like "sehen" (to see), "hören" (to hear), or "fühlen" (to feel).

Examples:

  • "Ich sehe das jetzt mit anderen Augen." (I see it differently now.)
  • "Ich fühle mich anders als gestern." (I feel different from yesterday.)
4. In comparison

- "andere" can be used in comparisons to mean "different from" or "other than". It can be used with comparatives like "besser" (better) or "schlechter" (worse).

Examples:

  • "Ich finde das Essen hier besser als in anderen Restaurants."
    (I think the food here is better than in other restaurants.)
  • "Ich bin anders als mein Bruder."
    (I am different from my brother.)
5. In idiomatic expressions

- "andere" is also used in various idiomatic expressions in German. Some examples include:

  • "Das ist eine andere Sache."
    (That is a different matter.)
  • "Mit anderen Worten..."
    (In other words...)
  • "Andere Länder, andere Sitten."
    (Different countries, different customs.)

Examples:

  • "Ich kann heute nicht zum Meeting kommen, aber das ist eine andere Sache."
    (I can't come to the meeting today, but that's a different matter.)
  • "Andere Länder, andere Sitten. Man muss sich anpassen."
    (Different countries, different customs. You have to adapt.)

Artikel im Dativ

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Artikel im Dativ" in German refers to the use of articles (determiners) in the dative case. In German, there are definite and indefinite articles, which have different forms depending on the gender, number, and case of the noun they modify.

2. Usage

- Here is some information about how articles are used in the dative case in German:

1. Definite articles

- The definite articles in German are "der" (masculine), "die" (feminine), and "das" (neuter) for singular nouns, and "die" for plural nouns. In the dative case, the articles change their form:

  • der -> dem
  • die → der
  • das → dem
  • die (plural) → den

Examples:

  • Ich gebe dem Mann ein Buch.
    (I give the man a book.)
  • Ich gebe der Frau eine Blume.
    (I give the woman a flower.)
  • Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel.
    (I give the child an apple.)
  • Ich gebe den Schülern Bücher.
    (I give the students books.)
2. Indefinite articles

- The indefinite articles in German are "ein" (masculine and neuter) and "eine" (feminine) for singular nouns, and "keine" for plural nouns. In the dative case, the articles change their form:

  • ein (masculine and neuter) → einem
  • eine (feminine) → einer
  • keine (plural) → keinen

Examples:

  • Ich gebe einem Mann ein Buch.
    (I give a man a book.)
  • Ich gebe einer Frau eine Blume.
    (I give a woman a flower.)
  • Ich gebe einem Kind einen Apfel.
    (I give a child an apple.)
  • Ich gebe keinen Schülern Bücher.
    (I give no books to the students.)

- In summary, when using articles in the dative case in German, the definite articles change their form depending on the gender and number of the noun they modify, while the indefinite articles change their form depending on the gender, number, and case of the noun. It's important to pay attention to the article forms in order to correctly convey meaning in German sentences.

1. Introduction

- "Artikel im Nominativ" in German refers to the use of articles (determiners) in the nominative case. In German, there are definite and indefinite articles, which have different forms depending on the gender, number, and case of the noun they modify.

2. Usage

- Here is some information about how articles are used in the nominative case in German:

1. Definite articles

- The definite articles in German are "der" (masculine), "die" (feminine), and "das" (neuter) for singular nouns, and "die" for plural nouns. In the nominative case, the articles have the following forms:

  • "der" for masculine singular nouns
  • "die" for feminine singular and plural nouns
  • "das" for neuter singular nouns
  • "die" for plural nouns

Examples:

  • "Der Mann trinkt Wasser."
    (The man is drinking water.)
  • "Die Frau isst einen Apfel."
    (The woman is eating an apple.)
  • "Das Kind spielt mit einem Ball."
    (The child is playing with a ball.)
  • "Die Studenten lernen Deutsch."
    (The students are learning German.)
2. Indefinite articles

- The indefinite articles in German are "ein" (masculine and neuter) and "eine" (feminine) for singular nouns, and "keine" for plural nouns. In the nominative case, the articles have the following forms:

  • "ein" for masculine singular nouns
  • "eine" for feminine singular nouns
  • "ein" for neuter singular nouns
  • "keine" for plural nouns

Examples:

  • "Ein Mann trinkt Wasser."
    (A man is drinking water.)
  • "Eine Frau isst einen Apfel."
    (A woman is eating an apple.)
  • "Ein Kind spielt mit einem Ball."
    (A child is playing with a ball.)
  • "Keine Studenten lernen Deutsch."
    (No students are learning German.)

- In summary, when using articles in the nominative case in German, the definite articles have different forms depending on the gender and number of the noun they modify, while the indefinite articles have different forms depending on the gender, number, and case of the noun. It's important to pay attention to the article forms in order to correctly convey meaning in German sentences.

Artikel und Pronomen im Nom Akk und Dativ

Table Of Contents:

1. Introduction

- In German, articles and pronouns change depending on the case they are used in. The three cases in German are nominative, accusative, and dative.

2. Usage

- Here is a brief explanation of how articles and pronouns change in each case:

1. Nominative Case

- In the nominative case, the articles and pronouns are not declined. Here are the articles and pronouns in the nominative case:

  • Definite articles: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter), die (plural)
  • Indefinite articles: ein (masculine/neuter), eine (feminine), keine (plural)
  • Personal pronouns: ich (I), du (you), er (he), sie (she), es (it), wir (we), ihr (you all), sie (they)

Examples:

  • Der Hund bellt.
    (The dog is barking.)
  • Ich esse eine Pizza.
    (I am eating a pizza.)
  • Sie sind meine Freunde.
    (They are my friends.)
2. Accusative Case

- In the accusative case, the definite article "der" → "den", the indefinite article "ein" → "einen", and the pronoun "er" → "ihn". Here are the articles and pronouns in the accusative case:

  • Definite articles: den (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter), die (plural)
  • Indefinite articles: einen (masculine), eine (feminine), keine (plural)
  • Personal pronouns: mich (me), dich (you), ihn (him), sie (her), es (it), uns (us), euch (you all), sie (them)

Examples:

  • Ich sehe den Mann.
    (I see the man.)
  • Er isst eine Banane. Ich sehe ihn.
    (He is eating a banana. I see him.)
  • Wir treffen unsere Freunde. Wir sehen sie später.
    (We are meeting our friends. We will see them later.)
3. Dative Case

- In the dative case, the definite article "der" -> "dem", the indefinite article "ein" → "einem", and the pronoun "er" → "ihm". Here are the articles and pronouns in the dative case:

  • Definite articles: dem (masculine), der (feminine), dem (neuter), den (plural)
  • Indefinite articles: einem (masculine/neuter), einer (feminine), keinen (plural)
  • Personal pronouns: mir (me), dir (you), ihm (him), ihr (her), ihm (it), uns (us), euch (you all), ihnen (them)

Examples:

  • Ich gebe dem Mann einen Apfel.
    (I am giving the man an apple.)
  • Er schreibt einem Freund einen Brief.
    (He is writing a letter to a friend.)
  • Wir helfen unseren Nachbarn. Wir geben ihnen Essen.
    (We are helping our neighbors. We are giving them food.)

Demonstrative Pronouns in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Dieser / Jener
  3. Der / Derjeniger / Derselber
  4. Demonstrative Adjectives and Nouns
  5. Declension Table: Demonstrative Pronouns

1. Introduction

- Demonstrative pronouns, also indicative pronouns, can replace previously mentioned nouns in a sentence. We use them to emphasise or distinguish something like this/that, these/those in English Grammar. In German grammar, demonstrative pronouns are declined to reflect case, gender and number. A different form is often prefered in spoken German.

2. Dieser / Jener

- Use dieser / diese / dieses and jener / jene / jenes to choose something specific out of a group.

Examples:

  • Welches Auto möchten Sie kaufen, dieses oder jenes?
  • Welches Kleid soll ich anziehen? - Dieses

- In spoken language, German speakers generally prefer to use der/die/das da or der/die/das dort instead of jener/jene/jenes,

Examples:

  • Möchten Sie diese Schuhe anprobieren? - Nein, lieber die dort.

3. Der / Derjeniger / Derselber

- Use der / die / das, as well as derjenige / diejenige(n) or derselbe / dieselbe / dasselbe to emphasise something.

Examples:

  • Wer ist der Junge? - Das weiß ich nicht. Den kenne ich nicht.
  • Derjenige, der das Rätsel zuerst löst, bekommt einen Preis.
  • Hat sie einen neuen Freund? - Nein, es ist derselbe wie neulich.

- The demonstrative pronouns der / die / das are declined in the same ways as relative pronouns. Pay attention to the dative plural.

Examples:

  • Wie geht es Jan und Linda? - Keine Ahnung, von denen habe ich lange nichts gehört.

4. Demonstrative Adjectives and Nouns

- We can also use demonstrative pronouns in front of nouns. In this case, they differentiate themselves from normal articles by emphasising something specific. Therefore, we also emphasise the demonstrative pronoun when speaking.

Examples:

  • Mit der Kleidung kommst du nicht in den Club!

(With a different outfit, you could get into this club; and maybe with this outfit you could get into another club, but not with this outfit in this club.)

Fragesätze

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Fragesätze" in German are question sentences that are used to ask questions. These sentences are formed differently from normal declarative sentences and usually start with a question word or a question particle.

2. Usage

- Here are some details about forming and using "Fragesätze" in German:

1. Question words

- Question words are used to ask questions about specific information, such as who, what, when, where, why, and how. In German, these words are "wer" (who), "was" (what), "wann" (when), "wo" (where), "warum" (why), and "wie" (how). They are typically placed at the beginning of the sentence, followed by the verb and the subject.

Examples:

  • Wer ist das? 
    (Who is that?)
  • Was machst du heute? 
    (What are you doing today?)
  • Wann kommst du zurück? 
    (When are you coming back?)
  • Wo wohnst du? 
    (Where do you live?)
  • Warum hast du das gemacht? 
    (Why did you do that?)
  • Wie geht es dir? 
    (How are you?)
2. Question particles

- Question particles are used to turn declarative sentences into questions. The most common question particle in German is "ob" (whether/if), which is used to ask yes/no questions. The particle is placed at the beginning of the sentence, followed by the subject and verb.

Examples:

  • Ob du kommst? 
    (Are you coming?)
  • Ob es heute regnen wird? 
    (Will it rain today?)
3. Inverted word order

- In German, the word order in a question sentence is inverted from the normal declarative word order. The verb usually comes first, followed by the subject.

Examples:

  • Hast du das Buch gelesen? 
    (Have you read the book?)
  • Kannst du mir helfen? 
    (Can you help me?)
  • Möchtest du einen Kaffee? 
    (Would you like a coffee?)
4. Modal verbs

- When asking a question with a modal verb (such as "können", "müssen", or "wollen"), the modal verb is placed first, followed by the subject and the infinitive of the main verb.

Examples:

  • Kannst du mir helfen? 
    (Can you help me?)
  • Müssen wir das machen? 
    (Do we have to do that?)
  • Wollen wir ins Kino gehen? 
    (Do we want to go to the cinema?)

- In summary, "Fragesätze" in German are question sentences that are formed using question words, question particles, inverted word order, and modal verbs. They are used to ask questions and gather specific information from the listener.

Grammatik

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Information

1. Introduction

- "Grammatik" in German refers to grammar, which is the system of rules that govern the structure and use of language.

2. Information

- Here is some information about German grammar:

1. Nouns and Articles

- In German, nouns have gender (masculine, feminine, and neuter) and number (singular and plural). Articles (determiners) must agree with the gender, number, and case of the noun they modify. There are definite and indefinite articles in German.

2. Cases

- German has four cases: nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive. Each case has its own set of endings for nouns, articles, and adjectives, and is used to indicate the function of a noun or pronoun in a sentence.

3. Verbs

- German verbs change their form depending on the tense, mood, and subject of the sentence. The most common tenses are present, past, and future, and there are several moods, including indicative, subjunctive, and imperative.

4. Word Order

- German word order is generally more flexible than in English, but it can still affect the meaning of a sentence. In main clauses, the verb usually comes second, while in subordinate clauses, the verb is placed at the end of the clause.

5. Adjectives

- In German, adjectives must agree with the gender, number, and case of the noun they modify. They can also be used as predicate adjectives, following a linking verb like "sein" (to be).

6. Pronouns

- German pronouns have different forms depending on the case and gender of the noun they replace. There are personal pronouns, possessive pronouns, reflexive pronouns, and demonstrative pronouns.

- In summary, German grammar is a complex system of rules that governs the structure and use of the language. Understanding the gender, number, and case of nouns, the forms of articles and adjectives, the verb forms and tenses, and the use of pronouns is essential to mastering German grammar.

Imperative Commands in German Grammar

Examples:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Conjugation

1. Introduction

- The imperative mood expresses requests and commands. We can use it to address people in the second person singular (du) plural (ihr) and polite form (Sie) as well as the first person plural (wir).

Examples:

  • Fahrgast: Halten Sie!
  • Fahrer: Steigen Sie ein!
  • Fahrgast: Fahren Sie mich bitte zum Bahnhof!
  • Fahrer: Schnallen Sie sich bitte an!
  • Fahrgast: Fahren wir!

2. Usage

- With the imperative, we order someone to do something.

Examples:

  • Halten Sie!
  • Steigen Sie ein!
  • Fahren Sie mich zum Bahnhof!

- Sometimes we include ourselves in the command and use the imperative for the 1st person plural (wir).

Examples:

  • Fahren wir!
Info

The imperative is very common in German, because it lets us say with the fewest words possible what someone should do. For non-native speakers, this form sometimes sounds rather rude, but it’s not usually meant that way. To sound more polite just say bitte (please).

Examples:

  • Fahren Sie mich bitte zum Bahnhof!
  • Schnallen Sie sich bitte an!

3. Conjugation

1st/3rd person plural (wir/Sie)

- We form the imperative for "Sie/wir" with the verb in the "infinitive form + Sie/wir". For the verb "sein", we add an additional "e".

Examples:

  • Gehen Sie! / Seien Sie ehrlich!
  • Gehen wir! / Seien wir ehrlich!
2nd person plural (ihr)

- The imperative for "ihr" is the finite verb form of the 2nd person plural, but without the pronoun.

Examples:

  • Geht! / Seid ehrlich!
2nd person singular (du)

- We normally form the imperative for "du" by removing the ending "en" from the infinitive. In elevated language we often add an e to many verbs, but in colloquial speech we generally leave it off.

Examples:

  • Geh(e)!/Sei ehrlich!
Irregular Conjugation in 2nd Person Singular:

- The root vowel change from "e" to "i/ie" also happens in the imperative; in this case, however, we never add the imperative-e ending.

Examples:

  • Lies! (lesen - ich lese, du liest)(not: Liese!)

- The root vowel change from "a" to "ä" does not happen in the imperative.

Examples:

  • Fahr! (but: ich fahre, du fährst)

- If the stem of the present-tense form ends in "d/t", we always add an "e".

Examples:

  • Warte! (not: Wart!)

- If the stem of the present-tense form ends in "consonant + m/n", we always add an "e". This doesn’t happen, however, if this consonant is an "m", "n", "l", "r" or "h" (but not "ch").

Examples:

  • Atme!/Zeichne!
  • but: Schwimm(e)!/Lern(e)!

- If the verb ends in "eln/ern", we always add an "e". (The e of eln/ern can be left off.)

Examples:

  • Fei(e)re! / Ang(e)le!

Conjunctions - Word Order in German

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Coordinating Conjunctions
  3. Subjunctions
  4. Conjunctional Adverbs
  5. Overview

1. Introduction

- Coordinating conjunctions connect two main clauses. Subordinating conjunctions and conjunctional adverbs connect main/independent clauses with dependent/subordinate clauses. Using subordinating conjunctions and conjunctional adverbs changes the word order in the clause.

Examples:

  • Kerstin ist glücklich, denn sie hat Urlaub.
  • Sie macht Urlaub an der Nordsee, weil sie das Meer liebt.
  • Sie will den Sonnenuntergang sehen, deshalb ist sie jetzt am Strand.

2. Coordinating Conjunctions

- In a clause that is introduced by a subjunction, the finite verb is placed at the end of the sentence (subjunction + subject + … + finite verb).

Some example subjunctions (secondary conjunctions) are: bevor, da, dass, falls, weil, wenn.

Examples:

  • Kerstin ist glücklich, denn sie hat Urlaub.

3. Subjunctions

- In a clause that is introduced by a subjunction, the finite verb is placed at the end of the sentence (subjunction + subject + … + finite verb).

Some example subjunctions (secondary conjunctions) are: bevor, da, dass, falls, weil, wenn.

Examples:

  • Sie macht Urlaub an der Nordsee, weil sie das Meer liebt.

- Dependent clauses that are introduced by a subjunction are called conjunctional clauses.

4. Conjunctional Adverbs

- In a clause that is introduced by a conjunctional adverb, the finite verb comes before the subject (conjunctional adverb + finite verb + subject + …).

Some example conjunctional adverbs are: dann, schließlich, trotzdem, zuvor.

Examples:

  • Sie will den Sonnenuntergang sehen, deshalb ist sie jetzt am Strand.

Modal Verbs in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Conjugation of German Modal Verbs
  4. Table of Conjugation

1. Introduction

- The modal verbs in German are dürfen (be allowed to/may), können (be able to/can), mögen (to like/may), müssen (to have to/must), sollen (to ought to/should) and wollen (to want to). Modal verbs express ability, necessity, obligation, permission or possibility.

Master the rules for conjugating modal verbs and get tips on how and when to use them in German.

Examples:

  • Max will Automechaniker werden. Dafür muss er viel über Autos wissen. Sein Vater soll ihm alles erklären. In der Werkstatt darf Max seinem Vater helfen. Max kann sogar schon Reifen wechseln.

2. Usage

- We generally use modal verbs with the infinitive of the full verb. The meaning of the sentence changes depending on which modal verb we use.

Examples:

  • Max will/darf/soll Automechaniker werden.

- If the full verb is assumed to be obvious from context, we often leave it off in colloquial speech.

Examples:

  • Kannst du Deutsch (sprechen)?

  • Willst du eine Pizza (essen)?

  • Ich darf das (machen).

3. Conjugation of German Modal Verbs

- To conjugate modal verbs in the present and simple past, we use the finite form of the modal verb. However, to conjugate modal verbs in the perfect tense, we use the infinitive form of the modal verb and full verb and the finite form the auxiliary verb.

Du musst schlafen.Du musstest schlafen.Du hast schlafen müssen.

- We only use the past participle of a modal verb in the present perfect and past perfect tenses in sentences without a full verb.

Examples:

  • Das habe/hatte ich nicht gewollt.

Nicht and Kein – Negation in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. When to use nicht
  3. When to use kein
  4. Using kein/nicht with sondern

1. Introduction

- Negation or negative sentences in German grammar are formed with the words nicht (not) and kein (no/none). The tricky part is understanding when to use nicht and when to use kein and where to put them in a sentence.

Learn about the word order of negative sentences in German and when to use nicht or kein.

2. When to use nicht

- We use nicht to negate sentences in German. Nicht can be placed in different parts of a sentence depending on what we want to negate or emphasise. We use nicht:

1. at the ende of a sentence with verbs in simple tenses i.e. the present or past tense.

Examples:

  • Er schläft nicht.

- but before the full verb in compound tenses i.e. the perfect tense

Examples:

  • Er hat gestern Nacht nicht geschlafen.
2. before the definite article or possesive pronouns used with nouns

Examples:

  • Er hat nicht das Essen bezahlt, sondern die Getränke.
  • Ich habe nicht seine Adresse, sondern ihre.
3. before names and proper nouns

Examples:

  • Das ist nicht Udos Auto, sondern Susis.
4. before pronouns

Examples:

  • Ich habe nicht dich gerufen, sondern Petra.
5. before adjectives

Examples:

  • Das ist nicht fair!
6. before adverbs

Examples:

  • Sie geht nicht gerne schwimmen.
7. before prepositions with indicators of place, time, and manner

Examples:

  • Wir wohnen nicht in Berlin.
  • Der Zug kommt nicht um 18 Uhr an.
  • Otto hat das Loch nicht mit dem Spaten gegraben.

To Note: Nicht almost always comes before the word it negates, unless it is negating a verb.

3. When to use kein

- We use kein in the negation of German sentences:

1. with nouns that don’t have an article

Examples:

  • Ich habe Hunger. - Ich habe keinen Hunger.
2. nstead of an indefinite article

Examples:

  • Das ist eine Katze. - Das ist keine Katze.

- The endings for kein match the endings of the possessive articles (see table below).

4. Using kein/nicht with sondern

- In comparisons with sondern we can use both kein and nicht.

Examples:

  • Ich habe nicht Kaffee, sondern Tee bestellt.
  • Ich habe keinen Kaffee, sondern Tee bestellt.
  • Sie hat sich nicht eine Jacke gekauft, sondern eine Hose.
  • Sie hat sich keine Jacke gekauft, sondern eine Hose.

Perfekt - Perfect Tense in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Perfect Tense

1. Introduction

- The perfect tense, also called present perfect (Perfekt), is a past tense. We use it to speak about actions completed in the recent past. In spoken German, the present perfect tense is often used instead of the past tense. We can translate the perfect tense using the English simple past tense.

Master the rules of conjugation for the perfect tense and get tips on when and how to use it.

Examples:

  • Gestern hat Michael sein Büro aufgeräumt.
  • Er hat sich vorgenommen, jetzt immer so ordentlich zu sein. Aber bis nächste Woche hat er das bestimmt wieder vergessen.å

2. Usage

- We use the German perfect tense to express:

1. a completed action in the past with the focus on the result of the action.

Examples:

  • Gestern hat Michael sein Büro aufgeräumt.

-> Result: the office is clean now

  • Er hat sich vorgenommen, jetzt immer so ordentlich zu sein.

-> Result: he doesn’t want to be so disorganised anymore

2. an action that will be completed by a certain point in the future.

Examples:

  • Bis nächste Woche hat er das bestimmt wieder vergessen.

-> The point in the future must be specifically designated, otherwise we use the future perfect.

3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Perfect Tense

- To conjugate verbs in the perfect tense we need the present tense form of sein/haben and the past participle (Partizip II).

Personsein haben
1st person singular (ich)ich bingegangenich habegelesen
2nd person singular (du)du bistdu hast
3rd person singular (er/sie/es/man)er ister hat
1st person plural (wir)wir sindwir haben
2nd person plural (ihr)ihr seidihr habt
3rd person plural/polite form (sie/Sie)sie sindsie haben

1. When to Use Haben or Sein

- The verbs haben and sein are used as auxiliary or helping verbs in the present perfect. Sometimes it can be difficult to know which verb to use. Luckily, there are a few rules for the usage of haben and sein in the German present perfect tense.

- We use haben to conjugate the present perfect with:

a. verbs that take an accusative object

Examples:

  • Michael hat das Büro aufgeräumt.
b. verbs without an accusative object that don’t express a change of state or place

Examples:

  • Er hat aufgeräumt.
c. reflexive verbs

Examples:

  • Das Büro hat sich verändert.

- We use sein to conjugate the present perfect with:

a. verbs of movement that don’t take an accusative object: gehen, laufen, fahren, fallen, fliegen, kommen, reisen, stolpern, stürzen

Examples:

  • Alle Kollegen sind in sein Büro gekommen.
b. verbs that express a change of state: aufwachen/erwachen, einschlafen, gefrieren, tauen, sterbn, zerfallen

Examples:

  • Michaels Ordungsliebe ist erwacht.
c. the following verbs: bleiben, geschehen, gelingen, misslingen, sein, werden

Examples:

  • Was ist mit Michael geschehen?

2. Past Participle

The past participle (Partizip II) is formed in the following ways:

a. Regular Verbs also known as weak verbs (schwache Verben) form the past participle with ge…t and the verb stem.

Examples:

  • lernen - gelernt
b. Irregular verbs are verbs that change their verb stem in simlpe past and/or the participle form (see list of irregular verb). There are two kinds of irregular verbs in German grammar: strong verbs (starke Verben) and mixed verbs (gemischte Verben).

- Strong Verbs form the past particple with mit ge…en.

Examples:

  • sehen - gesehen (sehen-sah-gesehen)
  • gehen - gegangen (gehen-ging-gegangen)

- Mixed Verbs form the past participle with ge…t.

Examples:

  • haben - gehabt (haben-hatte-gehabt)
  • bringen - gebracht (bringen-brachte-gebracht)

3. Exceptions
a. We add an -et to weak/mixed verbs when the word stem ends in d/t

Examples:

  • warten - gewartet
b. Verbs that end in -ieren form their past participle without ge.

Examples:

  • studieren - studiert
c. Inseparable verbs form the past participle without ge.

Examples:

  • verstehen - verstanden
d. For separable verbs, the ge comes after the prefix.

Examples:

  • ankommen - angekommen

- Personal Pronouns replace nouns that have already been mentioned. In German grammar, personal pronouns are declined depending on the case they are in (see below: table of personal pronouns in nominative accusative and dative). We use personal pronouns to talk about ourselves and to address other people.

2. Usage

- Personal pronouns have a different form for each grammatical person. They can reflect gender or number. We use personal pronouns in German grammar to express different things:

1. We use personal pronouns in the 3rd person (er, sie, es) to replace a previously mentioned noun.

Examples:

  • Ich habe eine Katze. Sie ist sehr niedlich.

- To avoid misunderstandings, it should always be clear which noun we are replacing (in case of doubt, it’s better to just repeat the noun).

  • Herr Schneider hatte einen Wellensittich. Er ist gestorben.
    (Who - the budgerigar or Herr Schneider?)
2. We use pronouns in the 3rd person neuter (es) in impersonal forms.

Examples:

  • Es regnet. Es ist schon spät.
3. We can also es as a placeholder for an entire clause that comes later in the sentence.

Examples:

  • Es freut mich, dass du mich besuchst.
    (instead of: Dass du mich besuchst, freut mich.)
4. We use personal pronouns in the first person (ich, wir) to talk about ourselves in singualr (ich) or plural (wir)

Examples:

  • Ich habe Hunger. Mir ist kalt.
  • Wir gehen ins Kino. Uns ist das egal.
5. We use personal pronouns in the 2nd person (du, ihr) or the polite form Sie (identical to the 3rd personal plural, except that the pronoun is written with a capital letter) to address other people,.

Examples:

  • Wie heißt du? Wie geht es dir?
  • Woher kommt ihr? Welche Musik gefällt euch?
  • Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Kann ich Ihnen helfen?

Plural Nouns in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Plural Noun Endings in German Grammar

1. Introduction

- A plural noun expresses that there is more than one person, object, idea etc. To form plural nouns in German, we can add -n/-en, -e, -r/-er, or -s to the end of the noun. The rules for plural noun formation in German grammar are listed below.

Examples:

  • die Geldscheine
  • die Münzen
  • das Geld (no plural)

2. Plural Noun Endings in German Grammar

- German plurals are formed by adding -n/-en, -e, -r/-er, -s. Some nouns are the same in their singular and plural forms. The ending of a nouns give us a clue as to which plural ending to use.

Examples:

  • die Löffel whilst others are mostly used in the singular
  • die Milch or plural form
  • die Eltern

- Below is a summary of word endings and their typical plural endings. Be aware that there are many exceptions to these rules.

1. Add "-n/-en"

Here is a list of German noun endings that form the plural with -n or -en:

a. masculine nouns with the endings -e, -ent, and, -ant, -ist, -or

Examples:

  • der Student - die Studenten
b. feminine nouns with the endings -e, -in, -ion, -ik, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tät, -ung

Examples:

  • die Nation - die Nationen

- In the case of feminine nouns that end in -in, the n is doubled

Examples:

  • die Lehrerin - die Lehrerinnen
c. the endings -ma, -um, -us in foreign words are usually replaced by -en

Examples:

  • das Thema - die Themen
2. Add "-e"

Here is a list of German noun endings that form the plural with -e

a. masculine nouns with the endings -eur, -ich, -ier, -ig, -ling, -ör

Examples:

  • der Friseur - die Friseure
b. many single-syllable feminine nouns

Examples:

  • die Hand - die Hände

(an umlaut is added to the plural form)

3. Add "-r/-er"

Here is a list of German noun endings that form the plural with -r or -er

a. many single-syllable neuter nouns

Examples:

  • das Wort - die Wörter

(an umlaut is often added to the plural form)

b. To note: feminine nouns never form the plural with -r/-er.

4. Add "-s"

Here is a list of German nouns endings that form the plural with -s

a. masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns with the endings -a, -i, -o, -u, -y

Examples:

  • der Opa - die Opas
  • das Auto - die Autos
  • die Mutti - die Muttis
  • das Hobby - die Hobby
b. family names

Examples:

  • die Lehmanns
5. No Plural Ending

Here is a list of German noun endings that don’t change in the plural form:

a. masculine nouns with the endings -el, -en, -er

Examples:

  • der Löffel - die Löffel
b. neuter nouns with the endings -chen, -lein

Examples:

  • das Mädchen - die Mädchen
6. Singular or Plural

a. Most nouns can be used in the singular and the plural.

Examples:

  • der Geldschein - die Geldscheine
  • die Münze - die Münzen
b. Some nouns tend to be used only in the singular

Examples:

  • das Geld
  • der Hunger
  • die Milch

(There is a plural form, “die Gelder”, but this has a different meaning.)

c. Some nouns are used only in the plural.

Examples:

  • die Eltern
  • die Leute
  • die Ferien

Imperfekt - Past Tense in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Past Tense

1. Introduction

- The past tense, also called simple past or imperfect (Imperfekt or Präteritum in German), is used to express facts and actions that started and ended in the past. It is typically used to tell stories or report past events in written German. In spoken language, it is common to use the perfect tense instead of the past tense. We can use the English simple past to translate this tense.

Examples:

  • Im letzten Jahr machte ich Urlaub in Deutschland.
  • Mit dem Fahrrad fuhr ich auf dem Elbe-Radweg von Hamburg bis Dresden. Die Strecke war fantastisch und ich hatte tolles Wetter.

2. Usage

- There are two ways to use the past tense in German, we can use it to express:

a completed action in the past

Examples:

  • Im letzten Jahr machte ich Urlaub in Deutschland.
  • Mit dem Fahrrad fuhr ich von Hamburg bis Dresden.
a fact or condition in the past

Examples:

  • Die Strecke war fantastisch und ich hatte tolles Wetter.
* The past tense in spoken German

- In everyday spoken German, it’s more common to use the present perfect to talk about the past.

Examples:

  • Im letzten Jahr habe ich Urlaub in Deutschland gemacht. Mit dem Fahrrad bin ich auf dem Elbe-Radweg von Hamburg bis Dresden gefahren.

- However, we still use the simple past of the verbs sein / haben to describe facts and conditions in the past.

Examples:

  • Die Strecke war fantastisch und ich hatte tolles Wetter.

3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Past Tense

- To conjugate verbs in the simple past, we remove the infinitive ending -en and add the following endings:

- Many strong/mixed (irregular) verbs change the word stem in the simple past. (see list of strong and mixed verbs: Starke Verben)

Examples:

  • gehen - ging, bringen - brachte

- If the word stem of a strong verb ends in s/ß/z, we either leave off the ending s, or we add an extra e.

Examples:

  • lesen - las - du last/du lasest

- If the word stem ends in d/t, we add an e before the ending for endings that begin with t/st.

Examples:

  • landen - ich landete, du landetest, er landete, wir landeten, …
  • bitten - ich bat, du batest, …, ihr batet

- If the word stem of a strong verb ends in ie, there is no ending e in the 1st/3rd person plural.

Examples:

Verben mit Dativ

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- In German grammar, there are many verbs that require a dative object. These verbs are called "Verben mit Dativ" (verbs with dative). Understanding how these verbs work is an essential part of mastering the German language.

2. Usage

- Here is a detailed explanation of verbs with dative objects in German:

1. Verbs with dative objects

- Verbs that take a dative object require an indirect object to complete their meaning. These verbs are often used to describe actions that involve giving or transferring something to someone else. Examples of such verbs include "helfen" (to help), "geben" (to give), "schicken" (to send), "sagen" (to say), "zeigen" (to show), etc.

Examples:

  • Kannst du mir bitte helfen?
    (Can you please help me?)
  • Ich habe ihm gestern das Buch gegeben.
    (I gave him the book yesterday.)
  • Meine Mutter schickt mir immer Pakete.
    (My mother always sends me packages.)
2. Word order

- When using verbs with dative objects, the indirect object usually comes before the direct object in the sentence. The word order is as follows: 

subject + verb + indirect object (dative) + direct object (accusative).

Examples:

  • Meiner Mutter habe ich gestern Blumen gekauft.
    (Yesterday, I bought flowers for my mother.)
  • Der Lehrer hat den Schülern die Hausaufgabe gegeben.
    (The teacher gave the students the homework.)
3. Pronouns

- In German, pronouns used as indirect objects are always in the dative case. Pronouns used as direct objects are in the accusative case. Examples of dative pronouns include "mir" (me), "dir" (you), "ihm" (him), "ihr" (her), "uns" (us), "euch" (you all), "ihnen" (them).

Examples:

  • Kannst du mir bitte das Buch geben?
    (Can you please give me the book?)
  • Ich habe ihr gestern geholfen.
    (I helped her yesterday.)
  • Er schickt uns immer Postkarten.
    (He always sends us postcards.)
4. Verbs with both dative and accusative objects

- Some verbs can take both a dative and an accusative object. The dative object indicates the recipient of the action, while the accusative object indicates the thing being acted upon. Examples of such verbs include "geben" (to give), "schicken" (to send), "sagen" (to say), "zeigen" (to show).

Examples:

  • Der Mann gibt dem Kind einen Ball.
    (The man gives the child a ball.)
  • Die Lehrerin schickt den Schülern eine E-Mail.
    (The teacher sends the students an email.)
  • Kannst du mir das bitte zeigen?
    (Can you please show me that?)

- In conclusion, understanding the usage of verbs with dative objects is crucial for mastering German grammar. With practice and patience, one can become proficient in using these verbs and constructing proper sentences in German.

- Adjective declension, also called adjective inflection, means that adjectives agree with a noun in gender, number, and case. Only attributive adjectives, adjectives that come before verbs, are declined in German Grammar. Predicative and adverbial adjectives don't change.

Examples:

  • Die kleine Katze liegt auf dem weichen Kissen des gemütlichen Sessels und träumt von einer großen Schale leckerer Milch.

Andere

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Andere" in German means "others" or "other ones". It is a pronoun that can be used in various ways depending on the context.

2. Usage

- Here are some common uses of "Andere" in German:

1. As a pronoun

- As a pronoun, "andere" can refer to people or things that are different from the one(s) already mentioned. It is often used in phrases like "einige andere" (some others), "viele andere" (many others), or "die anderen" (the others).

Examples:

  • Ich habe gestern ein Buch gekauft, aber ich will heute andere Bücher kaufen.
    (Yesterday, I bought a book, but today I want to buy other books.)
  • Er ist nicht wie die anderen Jungs in der Klasse.
    (He is not like the other boys in the class.)
2. As an adjective

- As an adjective, "andere" describes something that is different or distinct from something else. It can be used with or without an article, depending on the context.

Examples:

  • Es gibt andere Möglichkeiten, dieses Problem zu lösen.
    (There are other ways to solve this problem.)
  • Ich habe ein anderes Auto gekauft.
    (I bought a different car.)
3. As an adverb

- As an adverb, "andere" modifies a verb or adjective to indicate a difference or change. It is often used with verbs like "sehen" (to see), "hören" (to hear), or "fühlen" (to feel).

Examples:

  • Ich sehe das jetzt mit anderen Augen.
    (I see it differently now.)
  • Ich fühle mich anders als gestern.
    (I feel different from yesterday.)
4. In comparison

- "andere" can be used in comparisons to mean "different from" or "other than". It can be used with comparatives like "besser" (better) or "schlechter" (worse).

Examples:

  • Ich finde das Essen hier besser als in anderen Restaurants.
    (I think the food here is better than in other restaurants.)
  • Ich bin anders als mein Bruder.
    (I am different from my brother.)
5. In idiomatic expressions

- "andere" is also used in various idiomatic expressions in German. Some examples include:

  • Das ist eine andere Sache.
    (That is a different matter.)
  • Mit anderen Worten...
    (In other words...)
  • Andere Länder, andere Sitten.
    (Different countries, different customs.)

Examples:

  • Ich kann heute nicht zum Meeting kommen, aber das ist eine andere Sache.
    (I can't come to the meeting today, but that's a different matter.)
  • Andere Länder, andere Sitten. Man muss sich anpassen.
    (Different countries, different customs. You have to adapt.)

Direktionaladverbien

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- In German, "Direktionaladverbien" (directional adverbs) are adverbs that indicate direction or location.

2. Usage

- They are used to give information about where an action is taking place or in what direction something is moving. These adverbs are commonly used in combination with verbs of motion, such as "gehen" (to go), "fahren" (to drive), or "fliegen" (to fly).

Here are some examples of directional adverbs in German:

  • hierher (here, towards the speaker):
    Komm hierher!
    (Come here!)
  • dorthin (there, towards a specific location):
    Ich fahre dorthin.
    (I'm driving there.)
  • hinunter (downwards):
    Wir gehen die Treppe hinunter.
    (We're going down the stairs.)
  • herauf (upwards):
    Er kommt die Treppe herauf.
    (He's coming up the stairs.)
  • vorbei (past, by):
    Ich laufe am Park vorbei.
    (I'm running past the park.)

- Note that some directional adverbs can be separated into two parts, such as "hierher" (here + towards) and "dorthin" (there + towards).

- It is important to use the correct case with these adverbs, depending on the verb and the context of the sentence. In some cases, the preposition "zu" (to) or "von" (from) may also be used in combination with directional adverbs.

Fragewörter und Präpositionaladverbien

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- In German, "Fragewörter" (question words) are used to form questions. These words are often combined with "Präpositionaladverbien" (prepositional adverbs) to ask questions about location, time, manner, and reason.

2. Usage

- Here are some common question words and their English translations:

  • Wer? (Who?)
  • Was? (What?)
  • Wann? (When?)
  • Wo? (Where?)
  • Wie? (How?)
  • Warum? (Why?)

- These question words can be combined with prepositional adverbs to ask more specific questions.

Examples:

  • Mit wem? (With whom?)
  • In welchem Raum? (In which room?)
  • Um wie viel Uhr? (At what time?)
  • Auf welchem Berg? (On which mountain?)
  • Auf welche Weise? (In what way?)
  • Aus welchem Grund? (For what reason?)

- Prepositional adverbs are also used to give more specific information about location, time, manner, and reason. Here are some common prepositional adverbs in German:

  • Innen (inside)
  • Außen (outside)
  • Oben (on top)
  • Unten (at the bottom)
  • Links (on the left)
  • Rechts (on the right)
  • Drinnen (indoors)
  • Draußen (outdoors)
  • Morgens (in the morning)
  • Abends (in the evening)
  • Nachts (at night)
  • Langsam (slowly)
  • Schnell (quickly)
  • Wegen (because of)
  • Trotz (in spite of)

- Prepositional adverbs can be combined with verbs or used to modify nouns.

Examples:

  • Ich gehe langsam. 
    (I am walking slowly.)
  • Der Hund sitzt draußen. 
    (The dog is sitting outside.)
  • Wegen des Wetters bleibe ich zu Hause. 
    (Because of the weather, I'm staying at home.)
  • Der Mann auf der linken Seite ist mein Bruder. 
    (The man on the left is my brother.)

- Note that the case of the preposition changes depending on the context of the sentence, and it is important to use the correct case to convey the intended meaning.

Indefinite Pronouns in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Etwas/Nichts
  3. Jemand/Jeder
  4. Man
  5. Irgendjemand/Irgendetwas
  6. Declension Table: Jemand/Jeder/Man

1. Introduction

- Indefinite pronouns express something general or unspecific, rather than something concrete. When an indefinite pronoun is used, the subject or object of a sentence is not specifically defined.

Examples:

  • Kannst du etwas für mich tun? (general)
    (compared with: Kannst du mein Auto waschen?)

- Some of the indefinite pronouns in German grammar are etwas, nichts, man, jemand, jeder.

2. Etwas/Nichts

- The pronouns etwas and nichts are not declined - they do not change their form.

Examples:

  • Hast du etwas gehört?
  • Nein, ich habe nichts gehört.

3. Jemand/Jeder

- The pronouns jemand, jeder are declined.

Examples:

  • Ich sollte jemanden anrufen, aber ich weiß nicht mehr, wen.
  • Das kann doch jedem mal passieren.

- The pronoun jeder must also agree with the noun that it replaces.

Examples:

  • masculine - jeder
  • feminine - jede
  • neuter - jedes

4. Man

- The pronoun man is the equivalent of the English generic pronoun one or impersonal you. It becomes einem in the dative, and einen in the accusative. The possessive pronouns and possessive adjectives of man are the same as those of masculine 3rd person singular (er).

Examples:

  • So etwas macht man nicht! (nominative)
  • Ihre Stimme geht einem unter die Haut. (dative)
  • Der Stress macht einen krank. (accusative)
  • Man kann kaum sein eigenes Wort hören. (possessive adjective)

5. Irgendjemand/Irgendetwas

- To strengthen indefinite pronouns, we can insert irgend- before some pronouns, for example: irgendjemand/irgendwer, irgendetwas/irgendwas

Examples:

  • Irgendjemand/Irgendwer wird uns schon helfen.
  • Irgendetwas/Irgendwas hat er doch gesagt, oder?

Indirect Questions in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Word Order in Indirect Questions
  3. Indirect Questions with "ob"
  4. Punctuation in Indirect Questions

1. Introduction

- Indirect questions are questions that are included within the structure of another sentence. Because indirect questions are dependent clauses (Nebensätze in German), we have to change the position of the verb. Indirect questions follow certain introductory phrases, see the examples below. They often end with a full stop and not a question mark.

- Learn about the word order and punctuation of indirect questions in German grammar, then put your knowledge to the test in the exercises.

Examples:

  • Ich weiß nicht, …
  • Er fragt, …
  • Ich verstehe nicht, …
  • Sie möchte wissen, …
  • Ich sage dir nicht, …
  • Können Sie mir sagen, …

2. Word Order in Indirect Questions

- The sentence structure of indirect questions in German grammar differs from that of normal questions - in indirect questions, the finite verb is placed at the end of the sentence.

- The rule for word order in indirect questions is:

question-word + subject + object + verb.

Examples:

  • Wann hat er Zeit? - Ich weiß nicht, wann er Zeit hat.
  • Was hat sie gesagt? - Ich sage dir nicht, was sie gesagt hat.

3. Indirect Questions with "ob"

- If there’s no question word, we use ob to introduce in the indirect question.

Examples:

  • Kommt sie morgen? - Er fragt, ob sie morgen kommt.
  • Das kann doch jedem mal passieren.

4. Punctuation in Indirect Questions

- Indirect questions usualy end with a full stop and not a question mark (see example above). A question mark is only used when the indirect question is an actual question.

Examples:

  • Können Sie mir sagen, wie ich zum Bahnhof komme?

Komparation, Vergleichspartikel

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- In German, "Komparation" (comparison) is the process of comparing two or more things. This is done using "Vergleichspartikel" (comparison particles), which are used to form the comparative and superlative forms of adjectives and adverbs.

2. Usage

1. Comparison particles

- Here are some common comparison particles in German:

a. als (than) - used to compare two things

Examples:

  • Ich bin größer als du. 
    (I am taller than you.)
b. wie (as) - used to compare things that are equal

Examples:

  • Ich bin so groß wie du. 
    (I am as tall as you.)
c. am (the) - used to form the superlative

Examples:

  • Ich bin am größten. 
    (I am the tallest.)

- We use sein to conjugate the present perfect with:

a. verbs of movement that don’t take an accusative object: gehen, laufen, fahren, fallen, fliegen, kommen, reisen, stolpern, stürzen

Examples:

  • Alle Kollegen sind in sein Büro gekommen.
b. verbs that express a change of state: aufwachen/erwachen, einschlafen, gefrieren, tauen, sterbn, zerfallen

Examples:

  • Michaels Ordungsliebe ist erwacht.
c. the following verbs: bleiben, geschehen, gelingen, misslingen, sein, werden

Examples:

  • Was ist mit Michael geschehen?
2. Compare two things

- The comparative form of an adjective or adverb is used to compare two things. To form the comparative in German, add "-er" to the end of the adjective or adverb.

Examples:

  • alt (old) - älter (older)
  • groß (big) - größer (bigger)
  • schnell (fast) - schneller (faster)
3. Compare three or more things

- The superlative form of an adjective or adverb is used to compare three or more things. To form the superlative in German, add "am" before the adjective or adverb and "-sten" to the end.

Examples:

  • alt (old) - am ältesten (oldest)
  • groß (big) - am größten (biggest)
  • schnell (fast) - am schnellsten (fastest)
4. Comparison particles

- When using comparison particles, it's important to pay attention to the case of the nouns being compared. The nominative case is used when the things being compared are equal, while the accusative case is used when one thing is being compared to another.

Examples:

  • Der Apfel ist größer als die Orange. 
    (The apple is bigger than the orange.)
  • Mein Auto fährt schneller als dein Auto. 
    (My car drives faster than your car.)
  • Dieses Buch ist so interessant wie jenes Buch. 
    (This book is as interesting as that book.)
  • Meine Katze ist am faulsten von allen. 
    (My cat is the laziest of all.)

Conjunctions - Word Order in German

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Coordinating Conjunctions
  3. Subjunctions
  4. Conjunctional Adverbs
  5. Overview

1. Introduction

- Coordinating conjunctions connect two main clauses. Subordinating conjunctions and conjunctional adverbs connect main/independent clauses with dependent/subordinate clauses. Using subordinating conjunctions and conjunctional adverbs changes the word order in the clause.

Examples:

  • Kerstin ist glücklich, denn sie hat Urlaub.
  • Sie macht Urlaub an der Nordsee, weil sie das Meer liebt.
  • Sie will den Sonnenuntergang sehen, deshalb ist sie jetzt am Strand.

2. Coordinating Conjunctions

- In a clause that is introduced by a subjunction, the finite verb is placed at the end of the sentence (subjunction + subject + … + finite verb).

Some example subjunctions (secondary conjunctions) are: bevor, da, dass, falls, weil, wenn.

Examples:

  • Kerstin ist glücklich, denn sie hat Urlaub.

3. Subjunctions

- In a clause that is introduced by a subjunction, the finite verb is placed at the end of the sentence (subjunction + subject + … + finite verb).

Some example subjunctions (secondary conjunctions) are: bevor, da, dass, falls, weil, wenn.

Examples:

  • Sie macht Urlaub an der Nordsee, weil sie das Meer liebt.

- Dependent clauses that are introduced by a subjunction are called conjunctional clauses.

4. Conjunctional Adverbs

- In a clause that is introduced by a conjunctional adverb, the finite verb comes before the subject (conjunctional adverb + finite verb + subject + …).

Some example conjunctional adverbs are: dann, schließlich, trotzdem, zuvor.

Examples:

  • Sie will den Sonnenuntergang sehen, deshalb ist sie jetzt am Strand.

Konjunktiv II – The General Subjunctive in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Subjunctive II

1. Introduction

- The general subjunctive, also: past subjunctive or subjunctive 2 (Konjunktiv II), expresses hypothetical situations. It is also used in indirect speech and in polite questions and statements.

Examples:

  • Franz, wärst du so freundlich, an die Tafel zu kommen?

  • Ich wünschte, ich hatte Ferien. Wenn ich im Urlaub wäre, läge ich den ganzen Tag am Strand. Aber unser Lehrer sagt, wir müssten noch viel lernen ...

2. Usage

- We use the German subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II) for:

1. unreal or hypothetical wishes and hopes

Examples:

  • Ich wünschte, ich hätte Ferien.
2. unreal statements and conditional clauses (see conditional clauses)

Examples:

  • Dann könnte ich in den Urlaub fahren.
  • Wenn ich im Urlaub wäre, läge ich den ganzen Tag am Strand.
3. indirect speech when the subjunctive I can’t be used (see also indirect speech)

Examples:

  • Unser Lehrer sagt, wir müssten noch viel lernen.
4. polite or tentative questions or statements

Examples:

  • Wärst du so freundlich, an die Tafel zu kommen?

3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Subjunctive II

- There are two forms of the subjunctive II, one expresses situations in the present and the other situations in the past.

1. Situations in the Present

- To express situations in the present with the general subjunctive:

1. We add the subjunctive ending to the simple past stem (see table below, in the column finden). Strong verbs get an umlaut.

Examples:

  • finden (fand) - er fände
2. Weak verbs and some mixed verbs look the same in the subjunctive II as they do in the indicative simple past. Because of this, we generally use würde with these verbs (würde form).

Examples:

  • ich wartete - ich würde warten
3. In spoken German, the "würde + infinitive" is prefered for many strong verbs.

Examples:

  • gehen - ich ginge/ich würde gehen

- Prepositions indicate what kind of relationship other words have to each other e.g. place, time etc. They usually come before a noun in a sentence. Modale Präposition

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Modale Präposition" (modal preposition) is a type of preposition in German that describes the way in which an action or event is carried out. They are used to indicate the manner, means, or attitude with which an action is performed or an event takes place.

2. Usage

- Here are some common modale Präpositionen in German:

  • mit (with)
  • ohne (without)
  • durch (by, through)
  • auf (on, upon)
  • gegen (against)
  • um (around)
  • bei (at, near)
  • von (of, from)
1. Modale Präpositionen are often used with verbs to form what is called a "Präpositionaladverb" (prepositional adverb).

- Präpositionaladverbien describe how an action is carried out, and they are formed by combining a modale Präposition with an adverb.

- Here are some examples of Präpositionaladverbien using modale Präpositionen:

Examples:

  • mit Freude (with joy)
  • ohne Zweifel (without a doubt)
  • durch Zufall (by chance)
  • auf Deutsch (in German)
  • gegen den Wind (against the wind)
  • um die Ecke (around the corner)
  • bei Nacht (at night)
  • von Herzen (from the heart)
2. Modale Präpositionen can be used to indicate the manner in which an action is carried out in a sentence

Examples:

  • Ich gehe mit meinem Hund spazieren. 
    (I go for a walk with my dog.)
  • Sie arbeitet ohne Pause. 
    (She works without a break.)
  • Er spricht durch einen Dolmetscher. 
    (He speaks through an interpreter.)
  • Wir haben auf dem Berg gepicknickt. 
    (We had a picnic on the mountain.)
  • Er kämpft gegen die Krankheit. 
    (He fights against the illness.)
  • Sie geht um den See joggen. 
    (She goes jogging around the lake.)
  • Wir treffen uns bei McDonald's. 
    (We meet at McDonald's.)
  • Er schreibt von seiner Reise. 
    (He writes about his trip.)

- It's important to note that the modale Präposition used in a sentence can affect the case of the noun that follows it.

For example, "mit" takes the dative case, while "durch" takes the accusative case. It's important to learn which case is used with each modale Präposition to use them correctly in sentences.

Modalverben im Präteritum

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- In German, "Modalverben" or modal verbs are verbs that express modality or the attitude of the speaker towards the action being described. The modal verbs in German are "dürfen" (to be allowed to), "können" (to be able to), "mögen" (to like), "müssen" (to have to), "sollen" (to should), and "wollen" (to want).

2. Usage

- In the past tense or "Präteritum" form, the conjugation of modal verbs is irregular. The following table shows the conjugation of modal verbs in the Präteritum form:

ModalverbPräteritum
dürfendurfte
könnenkonnte
mögenmochte
müssenmusste
sollensollte
wollenwollte

Examples:

  • "Ich konnte nicht kommen" means "I couldn't come"
  • "Er durfte nicht mitkommen" means "He wasn't allowed to come along."

- It's important to note that the Präteritum form of modal verbs is not commonly used in spoken German, and the Perfekt form (formed with the auxiliary verb "haben" or "sein" and the past participle) is more commonly used in both spoken and written German.

Dependent Clauses in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Conjunctions
  3. Indirect Questions
  4. Infinitive Clauses
  5. Participle Clauses
  6. Relative Clauses
  7. Conditional Clauses
  8. Indirect Speech

1. Introduction

- Dependent clauses, also known as subordinate clauses or Nebesätze in German cannot stand alone as sentences – they always depend on an independent or main clause. Dependent and independent clauses are separated by a comma. Pay attention to the word order of dependent clauses – the finite or conjugated verb comes at the end of the clause.

Examples:

  • Ich weiß nicht, ob er dir hilft.

- When a dependent clause comes before a main clause, the main clause begins with the finite verb.

Examples:

  • Ob er dir hilft, weiß ich nicht.

2. Conjunctions

- We can join clauses together using conjunctions such as und, subjunctions like wenn, and conjunctional adverbs such as darum. In German grammar, different types of conjunctions require a different sentence structure.

Examples:

  • Sie ist Schweizerin und er ist Österreicher.
  • Wir lernen viel Deutsch, wenn wir nach Deutschland fahren.
  • Ich will Deutsch lernen, darum mache ich Urlaub in Deutschland.

3. Indirect Questions

- Indirect questions are questions that are included within the structure of another sentence. They usually come after certain introductory phrases.

Examples:

  • Er will wissen, wie spät es ist.
  • Ich weiß nicht, wo mein Handy ist.
  • Es würde mich interessieren, ob er uns morgen besuchen kommt.

4. Infinitive Clauses

- Infinitive constructions are used after certain certain phrases in German. They usually include the words zu or um … zu.

Examples:

  • Ich bin froh, das zu hören.
  • Er hat das getan, um uns zu helfen..

5. Participle Clauses

- Participle clauses are dependent clauses that use the present or past participle, although, they are not very common in German.

Examples:

  • Die Nachricht hörend, begann sie zu jubeln.
  • Den Zug erreicht, atmete er erleichtert auf.

6. Relative Clauses

- Relative clause alow us to give additional information without starting a new sentence. In German, relative clauses are always set off by commas.

Examples:

  • Das ist der Junge, der hier wohnt.
  • Das ist der Junge, den ich sehr mag.
  • Das ist der Junge, dem ich in Mathe helfe.
  • Das ist der Junge, dessen Eltern Schauspieler sind.

7. Conditional Clauses

- Conditional clauses show that an action will or would take place under certain confitions in the present, past or future.

Examples:

  • Wenn das Wetter morgen schön ist, gehen wir baden.

8. Indirect Speech

- We use indirect speech to report what other people have said.

Examples:

  • Er erzählte, er habe Urlaub in der Schweiz gemacht.

Passive Voice in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Conjugation of German Passive Voice
  4. Active or Passive

1. Introduction

- The passive voice has two forms in German grammar. The processual passive is conjugated with the verb werden and emphasises an action. The statal passive is conjugated with the verb sein and emphasises a condition. Who or what caused the action or condition is either not important, unknown or assumed to be general knowledge.

Examples:

  • Ein Mann wurde angefahren. Er ist verletzt.
  • Dem Verletzten wurde ein Verband angelegt. Jetzt wird der Mann ins Krankenhaus gebracht.

2. Usage

- We use the processual passive when we want to emphasise an action (What is happening?). Who is causing the action is unimportant or unknown.

Examples:

  • Ein Mann wurde angefahren.
  • Dem Verletzten wurde ein Verband angelegt.
  • Jetzt wird der Mann ins Krankenhaus gebracht.

(The most important information here is that someone was run down, bandaged up, and is being taken to hospital. Who ran the man down, applied the dressing, and is driving him to the hospital, is not important or unknown.)

- We use the statal passive to describe the condition (situation) after an action.

Examples:

  • Er ist verletzt.

(During the action, the man became hurt – now he is hurt.)

3. Conjugation of German Passive Voice

1. Processual Passive

- To conjugate the processual passive we need a form of werden and the past participle of the full verb. The rule for constructing sentences in the the processual passive is:

subject + form werden (+ object) + past participle

tenseexample sentence in processual passive
presentDer Mann wird verletzt.
present perfectDer Mann ist verletzt worden.
simple pastDer Mann wurde verletzt.
past perfectDer Mann war verletzt worden.
futureDer Mann wird verletzt werden.
future perfectDer Mann wird verletzt worden sein
2. Statal Passive

- To conjugate the statal passive we need a form of sein and the past participle of the full verb. The rule for construction sentences in the the processual passive is:

subject + form of sein + past participle

tenseexample sentence in statal passive
presentDer Mann ist verletzt.
present perfectDer Mann ist verletzt gewesen.
simple pastDer Mann war verletzt.
past perfectDer Mann war verletzt gewesen.
futureDer Mann wird verletzt sein.
future perfectDer Mann wird verletzt gewesen sein.

4. Active or Passive

- We use the active form to emphasise who or what is performing an action.

Examples:

  • Der Lehrer erklärte uns das Passiv.

- We use the passive to emphasise the action itself. Who or what is performing the action is often left off in passive sentences.

Examples:

  • Das Passiv wurde uns (vom Lehrer) erklärt.
1. Verbs that can’t form the passive

- Verbs with no accusative object can’t form the passive. Some of these verbs are:

1. verbs whose present perfect form takes sein (e. g. fahren)

Examples:

  • Ich fuhr selber nach Berlin.

  • Ich wurde selber nach Berlin gefahren. (Passive is impossible, because I drove myself.)

- But: fahren can also be used with haben + accusative object. In this case, a passive sentence is possible.

Examples:

  • Mein Vater fuhr mich nach Berlin.

(Passive: Ich wurde (von meinem Vater) nach Berlin gefahren.)

2. reflexive verbs

Examples:

  • Ich habe mich versteckt. (Ich bin mich versteckt worden.)
3. other verbs without an accusative object

Examples:

  • Er schläft. (Er wird geschlafen.)

- But: In colloquial speech we often use an impersonal passive (see exceptions), for example as an order.

Examples:

  • Jetzt wird geschlafen!

* Info

- Some verbs that have an accusative object can’t be used in the passive voice. For example, haben, kennen, wissen, es gibt.

Examples:

  • Ich habe einen Hund. (Ein Hund wird gehabt.)

  • Ich kenne die Frau. (Die Frau wird gekannt.)

  • Ich weiß die Antwort. (Die Antwort wird gewusst.)

  • Es gibt viele Museen. (Viele Museen werden gegeben.)

2. Turning the Active into the Processual Passive

- When we turn the active into the processual passive, the following things happen:

  • The accusative object becomes the subject.
  • The subject is left off, or only included as “von (+ dative)”.
  • The verb is used in the past participle form and we also need the helping verb werden in its conjugated form.
subjectfinite verbobjectinfinite verb
activeJemandverletztden Mann.
passiveDer Mannwird(von jemandem)verletzt.

- Example for all tenses:

tenseactiveprocessual passive
presentJemand verletzt den Mann.Der Mann wird (von jemandem) verletzt.
present perfectJemand hat den Mann verletzt.Der Mann ist (von jemandem) verletzt worden.
simple pastJemand verletzte den Mann.Der Mann wurde (von jemandem) verletzt.
past perfectJemand hatte den Mann verletzt.Der Mann war (von jemandem) verletzt worden.
futureJemand wird den Mann verletzen.Der Mann wird (von jemandem) verletzt werden.
future perfectJemand wird den Mann verletzt haben.Der Mann wird (von jemandem)verletzt worden sein.
3. Exceptions

- Only the accusative object can become the subject. If there is a dative object that needs to be moved to the first position in the active sentence, it stays in the dative.

  • active: Man legte dem Verletzten einen Verband an.

  • passive: Dem Verletzten wurde ein Verband angelegt.

- Active sentences without an object can also be made passive (impersonal passive). For this, we use the personal pronoun es or an adverbial modifier.

Examples:

  • Wir tanzten (gestern) viel. - Es/Gestern wurde viel getanzt.

Perfekt - Perfect Tense in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Perfect Tense

1. Introduction

- The perfect tense, also called present perfect (Perfekt), is a past tense. We use it to speak about actions completed in the recent past. In spoken German, the present perfect tense is often used instead of the past tense. We can translate the perfect tense using the English simple past tense.

Master the rules of conjugation for the perfect tense and get tips on when and how to use it.

Examples:

  • Gestern hat Michael sein Büro aufgeräumt.
  • Er hat sich vorgenommen, jetzt immer so ordentlich zu sein. Aber bis nächste Woche hat er das bestimmt wieder vergessen.å

2. Usage

- We use the German perfect tense to express:

1. a completed action in the past with the focus on the result of the action.

Examples:

  • Gestern hat Michael sein Büro aufgeräumt.

-> Result: the office is clean now

  • Er hat sich vorgenommen, jetzt immer so ordentlich zu sein.

-> Result: he doesn’t want to be so disorganised anymore

2. an action that will be completed by a certain point in the future.

Examples:

  • Bis nächste Woche hat er das bestimmt wieder vergessen.

-> The point in the future must be specifically designated, otherwise we use the future perfect.

3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Perfect Tense

- To conjugate verbs in the perfect tense we need the present tense form of sein/haben and the past participle (Partizip II).

Personsein haben
1st person singular (ich)ich bingegangenich habegelesen
2nd person singular (du)du bistdu hast
3rd person singular (er/sie/es/man)er ister hat
1st person plural (wir)wir sindwir haben
2nd person plural (ihr)ihr seidihr habt
3rd person plural/polite form (sie/Sie)sie sindsie haben

1. When to Use Haben or Sein

- The verbs haben and sein are used as auxiliary or helping verbs in the present perfect. Sometimes it can be difficult to know which verb to use. Luckily, there are a few rules for the usage of haben and sein in the German present perfect tense.

- We use haben to conjugate the present perfect with:

a. verbs that take an accusative object

Examples:

  • Michael hat das Büro aufgeräumt.
b. verbs without an accusative object that don’t express a change of state or place

Examples:

  • Er hat aufgeräumt.
c. reflexive verbs

Examples:

  • Das Büro hat sich verändert.

- We use sein to conjugate the present perfect with:

a. verbs of movement that don’t take an accusative object: gehen, laufen, fahren, fallen, fliegen, kommen, reisen, stolpern, stürzen

Examples:

  • Alle Kollegen sind in sein Büro gekommen.
b. verbs that express a change of state: aufwachen/erwachen, einschlafen, gefrieren, tauen, sterbn, zerfallen

Examples:

  • Michaels Ordungsliebe ist erwacht.
c. the following verbs: bleiben, geschehen, gelingen, misslingen, sein, werden

Examples:

  • Was ist mit Michael geschehen?

2. Past Participle

The past participle (Partizip II) is formed in the following ways:

a. Regular Verbs also known as weak verbs (schwache Verben) form the past participle with ge…t and the verb stem.

Examples:

  • lernen - gelernt
b. Irregular verbs are verbs that change their verb stem in simlpe past and/or the participle form (see list of irregular verb). There are two kinds of irregular verbs in German grammar: strong verbs (starke Verben) and mixed verbs (gemischte Verben).

- Strong Verbs form the past particple with mit ge…en.

Examples:

  • sehen - gesehen (sehen-sah-gesehen)
  • gehen - gegangen (gehen-ging-gegangen)

- Mixed Verbs form the past participle with ge…t.

Examples:

  • haben - gehabt (haben-hatte-gehabt)
  • bringen - gebracht (bringen-brachte-gebracht)

3. Exceptions
a. We add an -et to weak/mixed verbs when the word stem ends in d/t

Examples:

  • warten - gewartet
b. Verbs that end in -ieren form their past participle without ge.

Examples:

  • studieren - studiert
c. Inseparable verbs form the past participle without ge.

Examples:

  • verstehen - verstanden
d. For separable verbs, the ge comes after the prefix.

Examples:

  • ankommen - angekommen

Prepositions in German Grammar

  1. Introduction

1. Introduction

- Prepositions indicate what kind of relationship other words have to each other e.g. place, time etc. They usually come before a noun in a sentence. Prepositions can be tricky to learn because they cannot always be directly translated. Some German prepositions also indicate which case should follow them.

Examples:

  • Wegen einer Autopanne musste der Mann am Dienstagabend ohne sein Auto von der Arbeit nach Hause gehen.

2. Types of Prepositions

- Prepositions can be divided into different types depending on the relationship they show to another word in a sentence, for example, prepositions of place (locative) or prepositions of time (temporal).

Examples:

  • wegen einer Autopanne
  • am Dienstagabend
  • ohne sein Auto
  • von der Arbeit nach Hause
1. Prepositions of Place

3. Prepositions and Cases

- Prepositions in German grammar can indicate the case of the nouns, pronouns or articles that follow them. Some prepositions are always followed by the accusative case, others take the dative or genitive case. There are also two-way prepositions that can take either the accusative or dative case.

1. Prepositions That Take the Accusative

- The following is a list of German prepositions that are followed by nouns, pronouns and articles in the accusative case:

1. bis

Examples:
