1. Introduction

- The special subjunctive, also called subjunctive 1 or present subjunctive (Konjunktiv I), is primarily used in newspaper articles and reports when statements are repeated as indirect speech. The special subjunctive is also used in certain idiomatic expressions.

Examples:

  • Nachrichten: Hoch lebe das Geburtstagskind! Zu seinem 90. Geburtstag sagte der Schauspieler, er habe sich noch nie so jung gefühlt.

2. Usage

- The subjunctiv I is used to express:

1. indirect speech (in colloquial speech the indicative is more common; see indirect speech)

Examples:

  • Er sagt, er habe sich noch nie so jung gefühlt.
2. some idiomatic expressions

Examples:

  • Hoch lebe das Geburtstagskind!

3. Conjugation of German Verbs in Subjunctive I

- There are a few points to consider when conjugating the subjunctive I:

1.

- Only the verb sein is still common in all its subjunctive I forms: ich sei, du sei(e)st, er sei, wir seien, ihr seiet, sie seien

Examples:

  • Er sagte, sie seien im Kino.
2.

- We generally only use the subjunctive I in the 3rd person singular (er/sie/es/man) with all other verbs. We only have to remove the n from the infinitive.

Examples:

  • haben - er habe
  • schreiben - er schreibe
3.

- In the 2nd person (du/ihr), the only difference between the subjunctive I and the indicative is that there is an e before the ending in the subjunctive form.

Examples:

  • du träumst - du träumest
  • ihr geht - ihr gehet

- It is common to use the subjunctive II in the second person, instead of the subjunctive I because it’s easier to tell it apart from the indicative.

4.

- There is no difference between the subjunctive I and the indicative in the 1st person singular (ich), as well as the 1st and 3rd person plural (wir, sie) which is why we have to use the subjunctive II in this situation.

Examples:

  • "Sie gehen joggen." - Er sagt, sie gingen joggen. (subj. II)

Konjunktiv II – The General Subjunctive in German Grammar

  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- The general subjunctive, also: past subjunctive or subjunctive 2 (Konjunktiv II), expresses hypothetical situations. It is also used in indirect speech and in polite questions and statements.

Examples:

  • Franz, wärst du so freundlich, an die Tafel zu kommen?

  • Ich wünschte, ich hatte Ferien. Wenn ich im Urlaub wäre, läge ich den ganzen Tag am Strand. Aber unser Lehrer sagt, wir müssten noch viel lernen ...

2. Usage

- We use the German subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II) for:

1. unreal or hypothetical wishes and hopes

Examples:

  • Ich wünschte, ich hätte Ferien.
2. unreal statements and conditional clauses (see conditional clauses)

Examples:

  • Dann könnte ich in den Urlaub fahren.
  • Wenn ich im Urlaub wäre, läge ich den ganzen Tag am Strand.
3. indirect speech when the subjunctive I can’t be used (see also indirect speech)

Examples:

  • Unser Lehrer sagt, wir müssten noch viel lernen.
4. polite or tentative questions or statements

Examples:

  • Wärst du so freundlich, an die Tafel zu kommen?

- There are two forms of the subjunctive II, one expresses situations in the present and the other situations in the past.

Examples:

  • ich wartete - ich würde warten
3. In spoken German, the "würde + infinitive" is prefered for many strong verbs.

Examples:

  • gehen - ich ginge/ich würde gehen

1. Introduction

- "Konjunktiv II werden Infinitiv" (Subjunctive II with "werden" and Infinitive) is a grammatical construction in German that is used to express hypothetical situations, wishes, desires, or unreal conditions in the present or future. It is formed by using the subjunctive II form of the verb "werden" (would) followed by the infinitive of the main verb.

2. Usage

- It is formed by using the subjunctive II form of the verb "werden" (would) followed by the infinitive of the main verb.

1. Hypothetical situations.

Examples:

  • Ich würde gerne nach Berlin fahren.
    (If I were rich, I would travel around the world.)
2. Wishes and desires.

Examples:

  • Ich wünschte, ich könnte fließend Deutsch sprechen.
    (I wish I could speak German fluently.)
3. Unreal conditions in the present or future.

Examples:

  • Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, würde ich mehr Bücher lesen.
    (If I had more time, I would read more books.)

3.Structure

- The formation of "Konjunktiv II werden Infinitiv" is as follows:

1. Take the subjunctive II form of the verb "werden".

Examples:

  • ich würde
  • du würdest
  • er/sie/es würde
  • wir würden
  • ihr würdet
  • sie/Sie würden

- Note that the formation of the subjunctive II form of the verb "werden" follows regular conjugation rules for weak verbs. The infinitive of the main verb remains unchanged.

2. Add the infinitive form of the main verb at the end of the sentence.

Examples:

  • Ich würde gerne nach Berlin fahren.
    (I would like to go to Berlin.)
  • Er würde gerne Deutsch lernen.
    (He would like to learn German.)
  • Sie würden lieber zu Hause bleiben.
    (They would prefer to stay at home.)

- In summary, "Konjunktiv II werden Infinitiv" is a useful construction in German for expressing hypothetical situations, wishes, desires, or unreal conditions in the present or future. It requires the use of the subjunctive II form of "werden" followed by the infinitive of the main verb.

Nebensatz finale kausale konsekutive Nebensätze

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- In German grammar, "Nebensätze" or dependent clauses are subordinate clauses that cannot stand alone as a sentence. They are often introduced by a subordinating conjunction and express a specific relationship to the main clause.

- "Finale Nebensätze" are dependent clauses that express a purpose or goal, while "kausale Nebensätze" express a cause, and "konsekutive Nebensätze" express a result or consequence.

2. Usage

1. Finale Nebensätze (Final dependent clauses)

- Final dependent clauses express the purpose or goal of the main clause. They answer the question "Why?" or "For what purpose?". They are introduced by subordinating conjunctions such as "damit", "um...zu", "auf dass", or "zwecks", among others.

Examples:

  • Ich gehe ins Fitnessstudio, damit ich fit bleibe.
    (I go to the gym in order to stay fit.)
  • Er lernt Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten.
    (He is learning German in order to work in Germany.)
  • Wir sparen Geld, auf dass wir nächstes Jahr in den Urlaub fahren können.
    (We are saving money so that we can go on vacation next year.)
2. Kausale Nebensätze (Causal dependent clauses)

- Causal dependent clauses express the cause or reason for the action in the main clause. They answer the question "Why?" or "Because of what?". They are introduced by subordinating conjunctions such as "weil," "da," "denn," or "nämlich."

Examples:

  • Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
    (I am staying home because I am sick.)
  • Er geht nicht in die Schule, denn er hat frei.
    (He is not going to school because he has the day off.)
  • Wir haben das Konzert verpasst, weil wir im Stau standen.
    (We missed the concert because we were stuck in traffic.)
3. Konsekutive Nebensätze (Consecutive dependent clauses)

- Consecutive dependent clauses express the result or consequence of the action in the main clause. They answer the question "What happened as a result?" They are introduced by subordinating conjunctions such as "so dass," "sodass," "damit," or "dass."

Examples:

  • Es hat so stark geregnet, dass die Straßen überflutet waren.
    (It rained so heavily that the streets were flooded.)
  • Ich habe zu viel gegessen, sodass ich Bauchschmerzen habe.
    (I ate too much, so I have a stomach ache.)
  • Sie hat so viel gearbeitet, dass sie erschöpft ist.
    (She worked so much that she is exhausted.)

- Understanding the different types of dependent clauses and how they function in relation to the main clause is essential in German grammar. Mastery of these concepts allows for greater precision in expressing ideas and conveying meaning in written and spoken German.

Negation eines Satzes

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Negation eines Satzes" in German grammar refers to the process of negating a sentence, or expressing the opposite of its meaning.

2. Usage

- In German, there are several ways to negate a sentence, including by using negative particles, adverbs, or verb forms. Here is a detailed explanation of each method:

1. Negation with "nicht"

- The most common way to negate a sentence in German is by using the negative particle "nicht", which is placed directly before the word or phrase that it negates.

Examples:

  • Ich gehe heute nicht ins Kino.
    (I am not going to the cinema today.)
  • Sie spricht nicht sehr gut Deutsch.
    (She does not speak German very well.)
2. Negation with "kein"

- The negative particle "kein" is used to negate nouns or pronouns, and it takes different forms depending on the gender and number of the noun.

Examples:

  • Ich habe kein Geld.
    (I don't have any money.)
  • Sie hat keine Zeit.
    (She doesn't have any time.)
  • Wir haben keine Bücher.
    (We don't have any books.)
3. Negation with "niemand" or "nichts"

- The pronoun "niemand" means "nobody", while "nichts" means "nothing". They are used to negate verbs or entire phrases.

Examples:

  • Niemand hat gestern angerufen.
    (Nobody called yesterday.)
  • Ich verstehe nichts von Mathe.
    (I don't understand anything about math.)
4. Negation with adverbs

- There are several adverbs in German that can be used to express negation, such as "niemals" (never), "selten" (rarely), or "kaum" (hardly). These adverbs are placed before the verb in the sentence.

Examples:

  • Ich gehe niemals ins Schwimmbad.
    (I never go to the swimming pool.)
  • Sie isst kaum Fleisch.
    (She hardly eats meat.)
5. Negation with verb forms

- In some cases, the negation of a sentence is expressed by changing the verb form, for example by using the "nicht" prefix in the past tense or by using the subjunctive form of the verb.

Examples:

  • Ich habe gestern nicht gearbeitet.
    (I did not work yesterday.)
  • Wenn ich viel Geld hätte, würde ich nicht arbeiten.
    (If I had a lot of money, I would not work.)

- In summary, negating a sentence in German can be done using different methods, including the negative particle "nicht", the negative pronoun "kein", negative adverbs, or negated verb forms. It is important to use the appropriate negation method depending on the structure of the sentence and the intended meaning.

Negation eines Satzteils

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Negation eines Satzteils" is a grammatical concept in German that involves negating a part of a sentence. In English, it is often translated as "negation of a sentence part".

2. Usage

- Negation is the process of negating a statement, and it can be accomplished in several ways in German. One common method is to use the word "nicht", which means "not". In order to negate a sentence part, "nicht" is placed immediately before the word or phrase being negated.

Examples:

  • Ich esse Pizza. (I eat pizza.)
    → Negated sentence part:
    Ich esse nicht Pizza. (I don't eat pizza.)
  • Sie trinkt Wein. (She drinks wine.)
    - Negated sentence part:
    Sie trinkt keinen Wein. (She doesn't drink wine.)

Partizip I und II - Present and Past Participle

  1. Introduction

1. Introduction

- A participle is a word formed from a verb. In German grammar, there are two kinds of participles; Partizip I is the present participle (similar to the gerund in English grammar), and Partizip II is the past participle (formed with -ed in English). We can use participles as adjectives, to shorten or replace clauses, or in the conjugation of compound German tenses.

Examples:

  • Frau Kunze wurde von einer Freundin in ein Café eingeladen. Die beiden haben sich lange nicht mehr gesehen. Nach ihrer Tasche greifend läuft Frau Kunze zur Tür.
  • In einem neben der Kommode stehenden Schirmständer steht ein Schirm. Den Wetterbericht gehört, weiß Frau Kunze, dass es heute nicht regnen wird. Deshalb lässt sie den zusammengeklappten Schirm dort stehen.

2. Usage

- The subjunctiv I is used to express:

1. Present Participle

- We use the German present participle or Partizip I:

1. instead of a sentence clause for one of two simultaneously occurring actions

Examples:

  • Nach ihrer Tasche greifend läuft Frau Kunze zur Tür.
2. as an attributive adjective (with an adjective ending)

Examples:

  • In einem neben der Kommode stehenden Schirmständer steht ein Schirm.

 

2. Past Participle

- We use the German past participle or Partizip II:

a. instead of a sentence clause which expresses that the action described with the participle took place before another action

Examples:

  • Den Wetterbericht gehört, weiß Frau Kunze, dass es heute nicht regnen wird.
b. as an attributive adjective (with an adjective ending)

Examples:

  • Deshalb lässt sie den zusammengeklappten Schirm dort stehen.
c. in compound tenses (present perfect, past perfect, future perfect)

Examples:

  • Die beiden haben sich lange nicht mehr gesehen.
d. in the passive voice

Examples:

  • Frau Kunze wurde von einer Freundin in ein Café eingeladen.

3. Forming the German Participles (Partizip I und II)

1. Present Participle

- The present participle is formed in the following way: infinitive + d (for all verbs)

 

Examples:

  • winken - winkend

  • lachen - lachend

2. Past Participle

- There are two ways to conjugate the past participle in German:

a. weak and mixed verbs: ge…t

Examples:

  • lernen – gelernt
  • nennen – genannt
b. strong verbs: ge…en

Examples:

  • sehen – gesehen

4. Exceptions

1. Present Participle

- With the verb sein, we add an extra "e" before the "n".

Examples:

  • sein - seiend

2. Past Participle
a. Many strong and mixed verbs change their stem in the past participle.

Examples:

  • gehen - gegangen
  • bringen - gebracht
b. If the word stem ends in "-d/-t", we add an extra et to weak and mixed verbs.

Examples:

  • warten - gewartet
c. Verbs with the ending "-ieren" form the past participle without "ge".

Examples:

  • studieren - studiert
d. Inseparable verbs form the past participle without "ge". (see separable/inseparable verbs)

Examples:

  • verstehen - verstanden
e. With separable verbs, the "ge" goes after the prefix. (see separable/inseparable verbs)

Examples:

  • ankommen - angekommen

Passiv Alternative Formen

1. Introduction

- In German grammar, the passive voice is often used to focus on the object of a sentence rather than the subject.

2. Usage

- The standard form of the passive voice is formed by using the auxiliary verb "werden" followed by the past participle of the main verb. However, there are alternative forms of the passive voice that can be used for stylistic variation.

1. The reflexive passive

- One alternative form of the passive voice is the reflexive passive, which is formed by using the reflexive pronoun "sich" in place of the direct object.

Examples:

  • Active: Die Katze frisst die Maus.
    (The cat eats the mouse.)
  • Passive: Die Maus wird von der Katze gefressen.
    (The mouse is eaten by the cat.)
  • Reflexive passive: Sich wird von der Katze gefressen.
    (The mouse is eaten by the cat.)
2. The impersonal passive

- Another alternative form is the impersonal passive, which is used to express a general statement rather than a specific action. It is formed by using the pronoun "man" followed by the verb in the third person singular.

Examples:

  • Active: Jemand hat das Fenster geöffnet.
    (Someone opened the window.)
  • Passive: Das Fenster wurde geöffnet.
    (The window was opened.)
  • Reflexive passive: Man öffnet das Fenster.
    (The window is opened.)
3. The impersonal passive

- There is also a form of the passive voice called the "Zustandspassiv", which is used to describe a state rather than an action. It is formed by using the verb "sein" in combination with the past participle of the main verb.

Examples:

  • Active:
    Der Kuchen schmeckt gut.
    (The cake tastes good.)
  • Passive:
    Der Kuchen wird gut geschmeckt.
    (The cake tastes good.)
  • Zustandspassiv:
    Der Kuchen ist gut geschmeckt.
    (The cake tastes good.)

- In addition to these alternative forms, there are also other ways to express passive voice, such as the "Periphrastische Passiv" and the "Vorgangs- und Ergebnispassiv". These forms are less commonly used and more complex, and are typically only taught at an advanced level of German grammar study.

- Overall, the alternative forms of passive voice in German allow for greater stylistic variation and flexibility in expressing meaning. However, it is important to note that the standard passive form using "werden" and the past participle remains the most commonly used and widely accepted form in both written and spoken German.

1. Introduction

- The passive voice in German can also be formed with modal verbs. Modal verbs express ability, permission, obligation, or possibility, and include words such as "können" (can), "müssen" (must), "sollen" (should), "dürfen" (may), and "wollen" (want).

2. Usage

- To form the passive voice with modal verbs, the modal verb is conjugated in the present tense and followed by the infinitive form of the main verb, which is always in its past participle form.

- The word "werden" is not used in this construction.

Examples:

  • Das Buch kann gelesen werden.
    (The book can be read.)
  • Die Arbeit muss erledigt werden.
    (The work must be completed.)
  • Die Aufgabe soll gelöst werden.
    (The task should be solved.)
  • Die Tür darf nicht geöffnet werden.
    (The door may not be opened.)
  • Das Problem will gelöst werden.
    (The problem wants to be solved.)

- In the passive voice with modal verbs, the modal verb retains its original meaning.

Examples:

  • Das Buch kann gelesen werden.
    → means: "The book can be read" 
    → and not "The book must be read"
    → or "The book should be read"

- It is also possible to use the perfect tense in the passive voice with modal verbs, in which case the modal verb is conjugated in the present tense and the past participle of the auxiliary verb "haben" is added before the past participle of the main verb.

Examples:

  • Das Buch hätte gelesen werden können.
    (The book could have been read.)

- In this construction, the modal verb retains its original meaning, but the auxiliary verb "haben" is used to form the perfect tense.

- It is important to note that not all modal verbs can be used in the passive voice. The modal verbs "mögen" (may), "möchten" (would like), and "sollen" (should) are rarely used in the passive voice, while "wollen" (want) and "dürfen" (may) are more commonly used.

- Passive voice in German can be formed using the auxiliary verb "werden" and the past participle of the main verb. In present tense, this is known as "Passiv Präsens".

- The general formula for forming the passive voice in present tense is:

  • du wirst
  • er/sie/es wird
  • wir werden
  • ihr werdet

Examples:

  • Passive voice: Das Auto wird vom Mann repariert.

  • Active voice: Ich sehe den Vogel.
  • Passive voice: Der Vogel wird von mir gesehen.

    - In these examples, the passive voice is used to shift the focus of the sentence from the subject performing the action to the object receiving the action.

TopicName: Passiv Präteritum Perfekt Plusquamperfekt Futur I und II
TopicTheory:
Passiv Präteritum Perfekt Plusquamperfekt Futur I und II

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- Passive voice, or "Passiv" in German, is used when the subject of the sentence is the receiver of the action, rather than the performer of the action. In German, the passive voice is formed by conjugating the auxiliary verb "werden" in the appropriate tense and adding the past participle of the main verb.

2. Usage

- Here's a detailed explanation of how to form the passive voice in different tenses:

1. Passive voice in Präteritum

- In the Präteritum tense, the passive voice is formed by conjugating the auxiliary verb "werden" in the Präteritum tense and adding the past participle of the main verb at the end of the sentence.

Examples:

  • Der Brief wurde gestern geschrieben.
    (The letter was written yesterday.)
  • Das Haus wurde vor fünf Jahren gebaut.
    (The house was built five years ago.)
2. Passive voice in Perfekt

- In the Perfekt tense, the passive voice is formed by conjugating the auxiliary verb "werden" in the present tense and adding the past participle of the main verb at the end of the sentence.

Examples:

  • Der Brief ist gestern geschrieben worden.
    (The letter has been written yesterday.)
  • Das Haus ist vor fünf Jahren gebaut worden.
    (The house has been built five years ago.)
3. Passive voice in Plusquamperfekt

- In the Plusquamperfekt tense, the passive voice is formed by conjugating the auxiliary verb "werden" in the Imperfekt tense and adding the past participle of the main verb at the end of the sentence.

Examples:

  • Der Brief war gestern geschrieben worden.
    (The letter had been written yesterday.)
  • Das Haus war vor fünf Jahren gebaut worden.
    (The house had been built five years ago.)
4. Passive voice in Futur I

- In the Futur I tense, the passive voice is formed by conjugating the auxiliary verb "werden" in the present tense, followed by the infinitive of the main verb and the participle "werden".

Examples:

  • Der Brief wird morgen geschrieben werden.
    (The letter will be written tomorrow.)
  • Das Haus wird in zwei Jahren gebaut werden.
    (The house will be built in two years.)
5. Passive voice in Futur II

- In the Futur II tense, the passive voice is formed by conjugating the auxiliary verb "werden" in the Futur I tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb and the participle "worden".

Examples:

  • Der Brief wird morgen geschrieben worden sein.
    (The letter will have been written tomorrow.)
  • Das Haus wird in zwei Jahren gebaut worden sein.
    (The house will have been built in two years.)

- It's worth noting that some verbs, called "Modalverben", have a slightly different passive form. The auxiliary verb "werden" is replaced by the appropriate form of the modal verb, followed by the infinitive of the main verb and the participle "werden". 

Examples:

  • Der Brief muss geschrieben werden.
    (The letter must be written.)
  • Das Haus kann gebaut werden.
    (The house can be built.)

- In addition, there are alternative passive forms, known as the "Vorgangspassiv" and the "Zustandspassiv". The Vorgangspassiv emphasizes the action, while the Zustandspassiv emphasizes the result or state. The Vorgangspassiv is formed by conjugating the auxiliary verb "werden" in the appropriate tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb and the present participle of "sein". The Zustandspassiv is formed by conjugating

Passiv Zustandspassiv

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Zustandspassiv" is a type of passive voice in German that describes a state or condition resulting from an action, rather than the action itself. It is often used to describe the current state of something, rather than who or what caused that state.

2. Usage

- To form the Zustandspassiv, you start with the auxiliary verb "sein" (to be) and add the past participle of the main verb. However, the main verb must be an intransitive verb, meaning it does not take a direct object. This is because the Zustandspassiv focuses on the state or condition resulting from the action, rather than the action itself.

subject + form of "sein" + past participle

Examples:

  • Der Kuchen ist gegessen. (The cake has been eaten.)
    → Here, "gegessen" is the past participle of the intransitive verb "essen" (to eat), and "ist" is the auxiliary verb "sein" in the present tense.
  • Die Tür ist geöffnet. (The door is open.)
    → Here, "geöffnet" is the past participle of the intransitive verb "öffnen" (to open), and "ist" is the auxiliary verb "sein" in the present tense.

- It is important to note that the Zustandspassiv is less commonly used than the Vorgangspassiv, which is the standard passive voice used in German to describe an action being done by someone or something else.

Examples:

  • Der Kuchen wird gegessen. (The cake is being eaten.)
    → Here, "wird" is the auxiliary verb "werden" in the present tense, and "gegessen" is the past participle of the transitive verb "essen" (to eat).
  • Die Tür wird geöffnet. (The door is being opened.)
    → Here, "wird" is the auxiliary verb "werden" in the present tense, and "geöffnet" is the past participle of the transitive verb "öffnen" (to open).

- In summary, Zustandspassiv is a type of passive voice used in German to describe the current state or condition resulting from an action, and it is formed using the auxiliary verb "sein" and the past participle of an intransitive verb. It is less commonly used than the Vorgangspassiv, which is the standard passive voice used in German to describe an action being done by someone or something else.

TopicName: Perfekt der starken und schwachen Verben sowie Mischverben
TopicTheory:
Perfekt der starken und schwachen Verben sowie Mischverben

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- In German grammar, the Perfekt tense is used to talk about completed actions in the past.

2. Usage

- It is formed by combining the auxiliary verb "haben" (to have) or "sein" (to be) in the present tense with the past participle of the main verb. The past participle is formed differently depending on whether the verb is a strong, weak, or mixed verb.

1. Strong Verbs

- Strong verbs are also called irregular verbs because they do not follow the regular pattern for forming the past participle. Instead, they change their stem vowel in the past participle.

- The past participle for strong verbs is formed by adding "-ge-" to the beginning of the stem and then adding "-en" to the end.

Examples:

  • sprechen -> gesprochen

Examples:

  • Ich habe gesprochen. (I have spoken.)
  • Wir haben gegessen. (We have eaten.)
  • Er hat geschrieben. (He has written.)
2. Weak Verbs

- Weak verbs are regular verbs that follow a predictable pattern for forming the past participle.

- The past participle for weak verbs is formed by adding "-ge-" to the beginning of the stem and "-t" or "-et" to the end.

Examples:

  • arbeiten -> gearbeitet

Examples:

  • Ich habe gearbeitet. (I have worked.)
  • Wir haben getanzt. (We have danced.)
  • Sie hat telefoniert. (She has made a phone call.)
3. Mixed Verbs

- Mixed verbs are a combination of strong and weak verbs.

- In the past participle form of mixed verbs, the stem vowel changes like in strong verbs, but "-t" or "-et" is added to the end like in weak verbs.

Examples:

  • lesen -> gelesen

Examples:

  • Ich habe gefahren. (I have driven.)
  • Wir haben gelesen. (We have read.)
  • Du hast gelogen. (You have lied.)

- It is important to note that some verbs can be both strong and weak, depending on the meaning of the sentence. 

Examples:

  • Strong verb: "halten" (to hold) means "to stop".
  • Weak verb: "halten" (to hold) means "to hold onto something".

- In summary, the Perfekt tense in German grammar is formed by combining the auxiliary verb "haben" or "sein" with the past participle of the main verb. The past participle is formed differently depending on whether the verb is a strong, weak, or mixed verb. Strong verbs change their stem vowel in the past participle, weak verbs add "-t" or "-et" to the end, and mixed verbs have both a stem vowel change and "-t" or "-et" added to the end.

Plural Nouns in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Plural Noun Endings in German Grammar

1. Introduction

- A plural noun expresses that there is more than one person, object, idea etc. To form plural nouns in German, we can add -n/-en, -e, -r/-er, or -s to the end of the noun. The rules for plural noun formation in German grammar are listed below.

Examples:

  • die Geldscheine
  • die Münzen
  • das Geld (no plural)

2. Plural Noun Endings in German Grammar

- German plurals are formed by adding -n/-en, -e, -r/-er, -s. Some nouns are the same in their singular and plural forms. The ending of a nouns give us a clue as to which plural ending to use.

Examples:

  • die Löffel whilst others are mostly used in the singular
  • die Milch or plural form
  • die Eltern

- Below is a summary of word endings and their typical plural endings. Be aware that there are many exceptions to these rules.

1. Add "-n/-en"

Here is a list of German noun endings that form the plural with -n or -en:

a. masculine nouns with the endings -e, -ent, and, -ant, -ist, -or

Examples:

  • der Student - die Studenten
b. feminine nouns with the endings -e, -in, -ion, -ik, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tät, -ung

Examples:

  • die Nation - die Nationen

- In the case of feminine nouns that end in -in, the n is doubled

Examples:

  • die Lehrerin - die Lehrerinnen
c. the endings -ma, -um, -us in foreign words are usually replaced by -en

Examples:

  • das Thema - die Themen
2. Add "-e"

Here is a list of German noun endings that form the plural with -e

a. masculine nouns with the endings -eur, -ich, -ier, -ig, -ling, -ör

Examples:

  • der Friseur - die Friseure
b. many single-syllable feminine nouns

Examples:

  • die Hand - die Hände

(an umlaut is added to the plural form)

3. Add "-r/-er"

Here is a list of German noun endings that form the plural with -r or -er

a. many single-syllable neuter nouns

Examples:

  • das Wort - die Wörter

(an umlaut is often added to the plural form)

b. To note: feminine nouns never form the plural with -r/-er.

4. Add "-s"

Here is a list of German nouns endings that form the plural with -s

a. masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns with the endings -a, -i, -o, -u, -y

Examples:

  • der Opa - die Opas
  • das Auto - die Autos
  • die Mutti - die Muttis
  • das Hobby - die Hobby
b. family names

Examples:

  • die Lehmanns
5. No Plural Ending

Here is a list of German noun endings that don’t change in the plural form:

a. masculine nouns with the endings -el, -en, -er

Examples:

  • der Löffel - die Löffel
b. neuter nouns with the endings -chen, -lein

Examples:

  • das Mädchen - die Mädchen
6. Singular or Plural

a. Most nouns can be used in the singular and the plural.

Examples:

  • der Geldschein - die Geldscheine
  • die Münze - die Münzen
b. Some nouns tend to be used only in the singular

Examples:

  • das Geld
  • der Hunger
  • die Milch

(There is a plural form, “die Gelder”, but this has a different meaning.)

c. Some nouns are used only in the plural.

Examples:

  • die Eltern
  • die Leute
  • die Ferien

Prepositions That Take the Genitive

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- Prepositions indicate what kind of relationship other words have to each other e.g. place, time etc. They usually come before a noun in a sentence. Prepositions can be tricky to learn because they cannot always be directly translated. Some German prepositions also indicate which case should follow them.

2. Usage

- The following is a list of German prepositions that are followed by nouns, pronouns and articles in the genitive case:

1. aufgrund/auf Grund, wegen

Examples:

  • Aufgrund/Wegen der Hitze fiel der Unterricht aus.
2. trotz, ungeachtet

Examples:

  • Das Flugzeug startete trotz/ungeachtet aller Warnungen.
3. anstelle/an Stelle/statt

Examples:

  • Anstelle eines Badeurlaubs machten sie Urlaub in den Bergen.
  • Statt der Suppe brachte der Kellner mir einen Salat.
4. beiderseits, diesseits, jenseits, abseits, entlang, oberhalb, unterhalb, außerhalb, innerhalb, längs, seitlich

Examples:

  • Entlang/Diesseits des Flusses stehen Bäume.
5. links, rechts, nördlich, östlich, südlich, westlich, unweit, weitab

Examples:

  • Er wohnt östlich/unweit der Grenze.
6. während

Examples:

  • Sie lernten sich während der Konferenz kennen.
7. anlässlich, angesichts, infolge

Examples:

  • Anlässlich seines 60. Geburtstages lud er Freunde aus der ganzen Welt ein.
  • Angesichts/Infolge der steigenden Preise müssen wir genau überlegen, was wir kaufen.
8. abzüglich, zuzüglich

Examples:

  • Der Preis versteht sich abzüglich des vereinbarten Rabatts, zuzüglich anfallender Transportkosten.
9. anhand

Examples:

  • Anhand der Grafik erklärte sie die Entwicklung des Konzerns.
10. aufseiten/auf Seiten

Examples:

  • Der Vorschlag stieß aufseiten der Opposition auf großen Widerstand.
11. mithilfe/mit Hilfe, dank

Examples:

  • Mithilfe/Dank der Lesebrille kann Opa endlich wieder Zeitung lesen.
12. zugunsten/zu Gunsten, zuungunsten/zu Ungunsten, zulasten/zu Lasten

Examples:

  • Das Urteil fiel zugunsten/zuungunsten des Angeklagten aus.
  • Sämtliche anfallende Gebühren gehen zulasten des Käufers.
13. um … willen

Examples:

  • Um des lieben Friedens willen vertrugen sich die Nachbarn wieder.

Präpositionen Reflexive Verben mit Präpositionen

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Präpositionen" are prepositions in German that are used to indicate the relationship between nouns or pronouns and other elements in a sentence. "Reflexive Verben mit Präpositionen" are reflexive verbs used with prepositions to describe an action that is performed on oneself or on others with a preposition.

2. Usage

- When using reflexive verbs with prepositions, the reflexive pronoun must match the grammatical case of the preposition. The following are some commonly used prepositions in German with examples of reflexive verbs that use them:

1. an (on, at)

Examples:

  • sich anlehnen (to lean on oneself):
    → Ich lehne mich an die Wand an. (I lean on the wall.)
  • sich interessieren an (to be interested in oneself):
    → Ich interessiere mich sehr an Kunst. (I am very interested in art.)
2. auf (on, onto)

Examples:

  • sich aufregen über (to get upset about oneself):
    → Ich regte mich über die schlechte Note auf. (I got upset about the bad grade.)
  • sich freuen auf (to look forward to oneself):
    → Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende. (I look forward to the weekend.)
3. mit (with)

Examples:

  • sich beschäftigen mit (to deal with oneself):
    → Ich beschäftige mich mit der Geschichte der Kunst. (I deal with the history of art.)
  • sich unterhalten mit (to talk with oneself):
    → Ich unterhalte mich gern mit Freunden. (I like to talk with friends.)
4. in (in, into)

Examples:

  • sich verlieben in (to fall in love with oneself):
    → Ich habe mich in ihn verliebt. (I fell in love with him.)
  • sich setzen in (to sit down in oneself):
    → Ich setze mich in den Sessel. (I sit down in the armchair.)
5. auf (for)

Examples:

  • sich vorbereiten auf (to prepare oneself for):
    → Ich bereite mich auf die Prüfung vor. (I am preparing myself for the exam.)
  • sich konzentrieren auf (to concentrate oneself on):
    → Ich konzentriere mich auf die Arbeit. (I concentrate on my work.)

- It is important to note that the preposition used in a reflexive verb can change the meaning of the verb entirely. 

Examples:

  • "sich freuen auf" means "to look forward to"
  • "sich freuen über" means "to be happy about"

-> Therefore, it is important to learn the appropriate prepositions and their meanings in order to use them correctly in reflexive verbs.

Plusquamperfekt - Past Perfect/Pluperfect Tense

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Forming the "Plusquamperfekt"
  4. Conjugation of German Verbs in Past Perfect Tense

1. Introduction

- The past perfect or pluperfect (Plusquamperfekt) expresses actions that took place before a certain point in the past. It is the German equivalent of the English past perfect tense. We use this tense in storytelling together with the simple past, to look back at something that happened before a past event.

Examples:

  • Beim Talent-Wettbewerb spielte Luise fehlerfrei ein schwieriges Stück auf der Flöte.

  • Sie hatte sehr lange geübt, bevor sie das Stück so perfekt spielen konnte.

2. Usage

- We use the German past perfect tense to describe: an action before a certain point in the past

Examples:

  • Sie hatte sehr lange geübt, bevor sie das Stück so perfekt spielen konnte.

3. Forming the "Plusquamperfekt"

- The following are the forms of "Präteritum Plusquamperfekt":

1. With "haben" as the auxiliary verb
 
Subject + hatte + past participle

- The past participle (Partizip II) is formed in different ways depending on whether we are conjugating a strong verb (ge…en) or a weak/mixed verb (ge…t).

Examples:

  • Ich hatte das Buch gelesen.
    (I had read the book.)
  • Wir hatten schon gegessen, als sie ankam.
    (We had already eaten when she arrived.)
2. With "sein" as the auxiliary verb
 
Subject + war/warst/war + past participle

- The past participle (Partizip II) is formed in different ways depending on whether we are conjugating a strong verb (ge…en) or a weak/mixed verb (ge…t).

Examples:

  • Sie war nach Berlin gereist, bevor sie nach München kam.
    (She had traveled to Berlin before she came to Munich.)
  • Ich war gestern spazieren gegangen, als ich ihn traf.
    (I had gone for a walk yesterday when I met him.)

 

    4. Conjugation of German Verbs in Past Perfect Tense

    - To conjugate the German past perfect (Plusquamperfekt), we need the simple past forms of sein/haben and the past participle (Partizip II).

    1st person singular (ich)ich wargegangenich hattegelesen

    2nd person plural (ihr)ihr wartihr hattet
    3rd person plural/polite form (sie/Sie)sie warensie hatten

     

    1. Past Participle

    - The past participle (Partizip II) is formed in different ways depending on whether we are conjugating a strong verb (ge…en) or a weak/mixed verb (ge…t).

    2. Exceptions
    a. Many strong and mixed verbs change their word stems in the past participle. (see list of strong and mixed verbs)

    Examples:

    • gehen - gegangen, bringen - gebracht
    b. If the word stem ends in "d/t", we add an "et" to weak or mixed verbs.

    • warten - gewartet

Demonstrative Pronouns in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Dieser / Jener
  3. Der / Derjeniger / Derselber
  4. Demonstrative Adjectives and Nouns
  5. Declension Table: Demonstrative Pronouns

1. Introduction

- Demonstrative pronouns, also indicative pronouns, can replace previously mentioned nouns in a sentence. We use them to emphasise or distinguish something like this/that, these/those in English Grammar. In German grammar, demonstrative pronouns are declined to reflect case, gender and number. A different form is often prefered in spoken German.

2. Dieser / Jener

- Use dieser / diese / dieses and jener / jene / jenes to choose something specific out of a group.

Examples:

  • Welches Auto möchten Sie kaufen, dieses oder jenes?
  • Welches Kleid soll ich anziehen? - Dieses

- In spoken language, German speakers generally prefer to use der/die/das da or der/die/das dort instead of jener/jene/jenes,

Examples:

  • Möchten Sie diese Schuhe anprobieren? - Nein, lieber die dort.

3. Der / Derjeniger / Derselber

- Use der / die / das, as well as derjenige / diejenige(n) or derselbe / dieselbe / dasselbe to emphasise something.

Examples:

  • Wer ist der Junge? - Das weiß ich nicht. Den kenne ich nicht.
  • Derjenige, der das Rätsel zuerst löst, bekommt einen Preis.
  • Hat sie einen neuen Freund? - Nein, es ist derselbe wie neulich.

- The demonstrative pronouns der / die / das are declined in the same ways as relative pronouns. Pay attention to the dative plural.

Examples:

  • Wie geht es Jan und Linda? - Keine Ahnung, von denen habe ich lange nichts gehört.

4. Demonstrative Adjectives and Nouns

- We can also use demonstrative pronouns in front of nouns. In this case, they differentiate themselves from normal articles by emphasising something specific. Therefore, we also emphasise the demonstrative pronoun when speaking.

Examples:

  • Mit der Kleidung kommst du nicht in den Club!

(With a different outfit, you could get into this club; and maybe with this outfit you could get into another club, but not with this outfit in this club.)

Indefinite Pronouns in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Etwas/Nichts
  3. Jemand/Jeder
  4. Man
  5. Irgendjemand/Irgendetwas
  6. Declension Table: Jemand/Jeder/Man

1. Introduction

- Indefinite pronouns express something general or unspecific, rather than something concrete. When an indefinite pronoun is used, the subject or object of a sentence is not specifically defined.

Examples:

  • Kannst du etwas für mich tun? (general)
    (compared with: Kannst du mein Auto waschen?)

- Some of the indefinite pronouns in German grammar are etwas, nichts, man, jemand, jeder.

2. Etwas/Nichts

- The pronouns etwas and nichts are not declined - they do not change their form.

Examples:

  • Hast du etwas gehört?
  • Nein, ich habe nichts gehört.

3. Jemand/Jeder

- The pronouns jemand, jeder are declined.

Examples:

  • Ich sollte jemanden anrufen, aber ich weiß nicht mehr, wen.
  • Das kann doch jedem mal passieren.

- The pronoun jeder must also agree with the noun that it replaces.

Examples:

  • masculine - jeder
  • feminine - jede
  • neuter - jedes

4. Man

- The pronoun man is the equivalent of the English generic pronoun one or impersonal you. It becomes einem in the dative, and einen in the accusative. The possessive pronouns and possessive adjectives of man are the same as those of masculine 3rd person singular (er).

Examples:

  • So etwas macht man nicht! (nominative)
  • Ihre Stimme geht einem unter die Haut. (dative)
  • Der Stress macht einen krank. (accusative)
  • Man kann kaum sein eigenes Wort hören. (possessive adjective)

5. Irgendjemand/Irgendetwas

- To strengthen indefinite pronouns, we can insert irgend- before some pronouns, for example: irgendjemand/irgendwer, irgendetwas/irgendwas

Examples:

  • Irgendjemand/Irgendwer wird uns schon helfen.
  • Irgendetwas/Irgendwas hat er doch gesagt, oder?

1. Introduction

- Personal Pronouns replace nouns that have already been mentioned. In German grammar, personal pronouns are declined depending on the case they are in (see below: table of personal pronouns in nominative accusative and dative). We use personal pronouns to talk about ourselves and to address other people.

2. Usage

- Personal pronouns have a different form for each grammatical person. They can reflect gender or number. We use personal pronouns in German grammar to express different things:

1. We use personal pronouns in the 3rd person (er, sie, es) to replace a previously mentioned noun.

Examples:

  • Ich habe eine Katze. Sie ist sehr niedlich.

- To avoid misunderstandings, it should always be clear which noun we are replacing (in case of doubt, it’s better to just repeat the noun).

  • Herr Schneider hatte einen Wellensittich. Er ist gestorben.
    (Who - the budgerigar or Herr Schneider?)
2. We use pronouns in the 3rd person neuter (es) in impersonal forms.

Examples:

  • Es regnet. Es ist schon spät.
3. We can also es as a placeholder for an entire clause that comes later in the sentence.

Examples:

  • Es freut mich, dass du mich besuchst.
    (instead of: Dass du mich besuchst, freut mich.)
4. We use personal pronouns in the first person (ich, wir) to talk about ourselves in singualr (ich) or plural (wir)

Examples:

  • Ich habe Hunger. Mir ist kalt.
  • Wir gehen ins Kino. Uns ist das egal.
5. We use personal pronouns in the 2nd person (du, ihr) or the polite form Sie (identical to the 3rd personal plural, except that the pronoun is written with a capital letter) to address other people,.

Examples:

  • Wie heißt du? Wie geht es dir?
  • Woher kommt ihr? Welche Musik gefällt euch?
  • Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Kann ich Ihnen helfen?

Prepositions in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Types of Prepositions
  3. Prepositions and Cases

1. Introduction

- Prepositions indicate what kind of relationship other words have to each other e.g. place, time etc. They usually come before a noun in a sentence. Prepositions can be tricky to learn because they cannot always be directly translated. Some German prepositions also indicate which case should follow them.

Examples:

  • Wegen einer Autopanne musste der Mann am Dienstagabend ohne sein Auto von der Arbeit nach Hause gehen.

2. Types of Prepositions

- Prepositions can be divided into different types depending on the relationship they show to another word in a sentence, for example, prepositions of place (locative) or prepositions of time (temporal).

Examples:

  • wegen einer Autopanne
  • am Dienstagabend
  • ohne sein Auto
  • von der Arbeit nach Hause
1. Prepositions of Place

- Prepositions of place or locative prepositions show the position or location of nouns, prounouns or articles.

3. Prepositions and Cases

- Prepositions in German grammar can indicate the case of the nouns, pronouns or articles that follow them. Some prepositions are always followed by the accusative case, others take the dative or genitive case. There are also two-way prepositions that can take either the accusative or dative case.

1. Prepositions That Take the Accusative

- The following is a list of German prepositions that are followed by nouns, pronouns and articles in the accusative case:

1. bis

Examples:

  • Kannst du das bis nächsten Montag erledigen?
2. um, um … herum, durch, … entlang

Examples:

  • Er geht um das Haus (herum).
  • Gehen Sie durch den Tunnel und dann die Straße entlang!
3. für, gegen, ohne

Examples:

  • Ohne dich haben wir keine Chance gegen die andere Mannschaft. Also nimm dir für den Sonntag nichts anderes vor!
2. Prepositions That Take the Dative

- The following is a list of German prepositions that are followed by nouns, pronouns and articles in the dative case:

1. aus, aus … heraus

Examples:

  • Er kommt aus dem Haus (heraus).
2. außer

Examples:

  • Außer mir war niemand auf der Straße.
3. bei, zu, bis zu

Examples:

  • Ich fahre zu einer Freundin und bleibe bis zum Sonntag bei ihr.
4. entgegen, entsprechend, gemäß

Examples:

  • Entgegen der Meinung des Wetterdienstes hat es heute doch geregnet.
5. getreu

Examples:

  • Er handelt immer getreu seinem Motto.
6. gegenüber, nahe

Examples:

  • Das Hotel befindet sich gegenüber dem Bahnhof.
7. mit, nach

Examples:

  • Nach der Arbeit fuhr sie mit dem Bus nach Hause.
8. samt, mitsamt

Examples:

  • Um Unkraut erfolgreich zu bekämpfen, muss man es samt/mitsamt der Wurzel entfernen.
9. seit

Examples:

  • Maria lernt seit einem Jahr Deutsch.
10. von, von … aus

Examples:

  • Von der Kreuzung (aus) ist es nicht mehr weit.
11. … zufolge

Examples:

  • Dem Bericht zufolge ist das Produkt sehr zu empfehlen.
12. … zuliebe

Examples:

  • Der Umwelt zuliebe trennen wir unseren Müll.
3. Prepositions That Take the Genitive

- The following is a list of German prepositions that are followed by nouns, pronouns and articles in the genitive case:

1. aufgrund/auf Grund, wegen

Examples:

  • Aufgrund/Wegen der Hitze fiel der Unterricht aus.
2. trotz, ungeachtet

Examples:

  • Das Flugzeug startete trotz/ungeachtet aller Warnungen.
3. anstelle/an Stelle/statt

Examples:

  • Anstelle eines Badeurlaubs machten sie Urlaub in den Bergen.
  • Statt der Suppe brachte der Kellner mir einen Salat.
4. beiderseits, diesseits, jenseits, abseits, entlang, oberhalb, unterhalb, außerhalb, innerhalb, längs, seitlich

Examples:

  • Entlang/Diesseits des Flusses stehen Bäume.
5. links, rechts, nördlich, östlich, südlich, westlich, unweit, weitab

Examples:

  • Er wohnt östlich/unweit der Grenze.
6. während

Examples:

  • Sie lernten sich während der Konferenz kennen.
7. anlässlich, angesichts, infolge

Examples:

  • Anlässlich seines 60. Geburtstages lud er Freunde aus der ganzen Welt ein.
  • Angesichts/Infolge der steigenden Preise müssen wir genau überlegen, was wir kaufen.
8. abzüglich, zuzüglich

Examples:

  • Der Preis versteht sich abzüglich des vereinbarten Rabatts, zuzüglich anfallender Transportkosten.
9. anhand

Examples:

  • Anhand der Grafik erklärte sie die Entwicklung des Konzerns.
10. aufseiten/auf Seiten

Examples:

  • Der Vorschlag stieß aufseiten der Opposition auf großen Widerstand.
11. mithilfe/mit Hilfe, dank

Examples:

  • Mithilfe/Dank der Lesebrille kann Opa endlich wieder Zeitung lesen.
12. zugunsten/zu Gunsten, zuungunsten/zu Ungunsten, zulasten/zu Lasten

Examples:

  • Das Urteil fiel zugunsten/zuungunsten des Angeklagten aus.
  • Sämtliche anfallende Gebühren gehen zulasten des Käufers.
13. um … willen

Examples:

  • Um des lieben Friedens willen vertrugen sich die Nachbarn wieder.
4. Prepositions That Take the Dative or Accusative

- Some prepositions take both the accusative and the dative in different situations. We use the accusative when we want to express motion (Where to?). We use the dative when we’re talking about a position (Where?).

  • an, auf, in, über, unter, hinter, neben, vor, zwischen
TO NOTE

- When we use the prepositions mentioned above as propositions of time (when?), they are always followed by the dative case.

Examples:

  • Wir treffen uns in einer Stunde.
  • An meinem Geburtstag sind wir ins Kino gegangen.

Reflexive Pronouns

1. Introduction

- Reflexive pronouns in German grammar are mich/mir, dich/dir, uns, euch and sich. We use them with reflexive and reciprocal verbs. Reflexive pronouns always refer to the subject and must be declined to match the case they are in.

2. Table of Reflexive Pronouns in Accusative and Dative

- Use the following table of reflexive pronouns in the accusative and dative cases to help you learn German reflexive pronouns.

dativemirdirsichunseuchsich

3. Usage

- We use reflexive pronouns with two different types of verbs in German grammar:

1. Reflexive verbs use the reflexive pronouns with the meaning "oneself".

- We use the reflexive pronoun in the dative if there is also an accusative object. (see also Reflexive Verbs)

Examples:

  • Ich dusche mich. (I see myself in the miriror – reflexive)

  • Ich putze mir die Zähne.

2. Reciprocal verbs use the reflexive pronouns with the meaning "each other".

- Therefore, we can only use reciprocal verbs in the plural. These verbs include among others: sich kennen, sich sehen, sich lieben, sich streiten, sich einigen

Examples:

  • Ich glaube, wir kennen uns. (= wir kennen einander) (we see one another; you see me, I see you – reciprocal)

  • Tom und Albert streiten sich. (= der eine mit dem anderen)

Redewendungen

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Redewendungen" in German grammar refer to idiomatic expressions or phrases that have a figurative or metaphorical meaning, which may not be immediately apparent from the literal meaning of the words. These expressions are an important part of the German language and can often be found in everyday conversations, literature, and other forms of communication.

2. Usage

- Redewendungen can be classified into different categories based on their structure and usage. Some common categories include:

1. Sprichwörter (proverbs)

- Sprichwörter (proverbs): These are short, pithy sayings that express a general truth or moral lesson.

Examples:

  • Aller Anfang ist schwer.
    (All beginnings are difficult)
  • Wer anderen eine Grube gräbt, fällt selbst hinein.
    (He who digs a pit for others, falls into it himself).
2. Redensarten (idioms)

- These are expressions or phrases that have a figurative meaning, which may not be immediately clear from the literal meaning of the words.

Examples:

  • Das ist ein Kinderspiel.
    (That's child's play)
  • Das kommt mir spanisch vor.
    (That seems like Spanish to me).
3. Metaphern (metaphors)

- These are figures of speech that use a word or phrase to describe something in a way that is not literally true, but that helps to create a vivid image or comparison.

Examples:

  • Der Tag bricht an.
    (The day is breaking)
  • Er hat einen kühlen Kopf bewahrt.
    (He kept a cool head).
4. Vergleiche (comparisons)

- These are expressions that use "als" (than) or "wie" (as) to compare one thing to another.

Examples:

  • Schnell wie der Wind.
    (As fast as the wind)
  • Hart wie Stahl.
    (Hard as steel).
5. Phrasen (phrases)

- These are groups of words that function as a single unit in a sentence.

Examples:

  • Im Großen und Ganzen.
    (On the whole)
  • In letzter Sekunde.
    (In the nick of time).

- It is important to learn and understand redewendungen in German language to improve one's communication skills and comprehension in daily life situations.

Relative Clauses

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Construction and Word Oder of Relative Clauses

1. Introduction

- Relative clauses allow us to provide additional information about a noun without starting a new sentence. We can also use them to combine two main clauses. Relative clauses are always introduced by relative pronouns, usually, der, die, das for people and things and not wer/wen (who/whom) as in English relative clauses. In German grammar, relative clauses are always set off by commas.

Examples:

  • Das sind die Freunde, mit denen ich viel Zeit verbringe. Bodo, den ich schon ewig kenne, ist sehr lustig. Toni, der eine Brille trägt, geht in meine Klasse. Linda, deren Lächeln bezaubernd ist, kann toll tanzen.

2. Usage

- We use relative clauses to give additional information about a subject or object, or to turn two main clauses into one complex sentence. The relative clause can be in the nominative, accusative, dative or genitive case.

Nominative:

  • Toni, der eine Brille trägt, geht in meine Klasse.

    • (Toni trägt eine Brille. - Wer?)

Accusative:

  • Bodo, den ich schon ewig kenne, ist sehr lustig.

    • (Bodo kenne ich schon ewig. - Wen?)

Dative:

  • Das sind die Freunde, mit denen ich viel Zeit verbringe.

    • (Mit den Freunden verbringe ich viel Zeit. - Mit wem?)

Genitive:

  • Linda, deren Lächeln bezaubernd ist, kann toll tanzen.

    • (Lindas Lächeln ist bezaubernd. - Wessen Lächeln?)

3. Construction and Word Oder of Relative Clauses

- To construct relative clauses in German grammar, we use relative pronouns or relative adverbs. They generally come directly after the subject/object to which they refer – this can be at the end of the main clause, or in the middle of the sentence. Relative clauses are dependent clauses so we have to pay attention to the word order and placement of the verb. The verb is always placed at the end of the relative clause.

1. Declension Table: Relative Pronouns

- Relative pronouns change form according to the gender and number of the noun to which they refer. The following table provides an overview of the declension/infelction of relative pronouns in the nominative, accusative, dative and genitive cases.

NominativeAccusativeDativeGenitive
masculine (m)der/welcherden/welchendem/welchemdessen
feminine (f)die/welchedie/welcheder/welcherderen
neuter (n)das/welchesdas/welchesdem/welchemdessen
plural (pl)die/welchedie/welchedenen/welchenderen

- Which case we use depends on whether the relative pronoun is replacing a subject or an object in the relative clause. Remember that we often have to use a different case in the relative clause than in the main clause.

Examples:

  • Bodo, den ich schon ewig kenne, ist sehr lustig.

    Bodo ist sehr lustig. (Wer? – nominative in main clause)
    Bodo kenne ich schon ewig. (Wen? – accusative in relative clause)

Usage of Relative Pronouns

- The relative pronouns der/die/das are generally prefered in everyday speech. Whereas, welcher/welche/welches are mostly used to avoid repeating the same word.

Examples:

  • Das ist die Frau, die die Post austrägt.

Better:

  • Das ist die Frau, welche die Post austrägt.

- A preposition can come before the relative pronoun.

Examples:

  • Das sind die Freunde, mit denen ich viel Zeit verbringe.
2. Relative Adverbs

- Relative adverbs do not change form. They often refer to an entire clause rather than a single noun. Some relative adverbs are was, wo, womit, wofür, worüber.

Examples:

  • Er spricht fünf Fremdsprachen, was mich sehr beeindruckt.
  • Ich warte dort, wo wir uns immer treffen.
  • Christian unterstützte mich, wofür ich ihm sehr dankbar bin.
  • Sybille besuchte uns, worüber wir uns sehr freuten

Satzstruktur

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. The main elements of Satzstruktur 
  3. The structure

1. Introduction

- In German grammar, Satzstruktur refers to the structure of a sentence, which includes the order and placement of words and phrases. The basic sentence structure in German is Subject-Verb-Object (SVO), but the word order can be changed to emphasize different parts of the sentence or convey different meanings.

2. The main elements of Satzstruktur 

- Here are the main elements of Satzstruktur in German:

1. Subject (Subjekt)

- The person or thing that performs the action of the sentence. It usually comes before the verb and can be a noun, pronoun, or phrase.

Examples:

  • Der Hund (the dog)
  • Mein Bruder (My brother)
2. Verb (Verb)

- The action or state of being in the sentence. It comes after the subject and can be in any tense or mood.

Examples:

  • spielt (plays)
  • bellt (barks)
3. Object (Objekt)

- The person or thing that receives the action of the sentence. It comes after the verb and can be a noun, pronoun, or phrase.

Examples:

  • Tennis (tennis)
  • den Postboten (the postman)
4. Adverbial (Adverbiale)

- Words or phrases that modify the verb or provide additional information about the sentence.

Examples:

  • heute Morgen (this morning)

 

3. The Structure

- The basic word order in a German sentence is:

Subject - Verb - Object (SVO)

Examples:

  • Der Hund bellt den Postboten.
    (The dog barks at the postman.)

- However, German allows for flexibility in word order, especially with the use of adverbials. Here are some other common sentence structures:

1.  Verb - Subject - Object (VSO)

Examples:

  • Bellt der Hund den Postboten?
    (Does the dog bark at the postman?)
2. Object - Subject - Verb (OSV)

Examples:

  • Den Postboten bellt der Hund.
    (It's the postman that the dog barks at.)
3. Verb - Object - Subject (VOS)

Examples:

  • Bellt den Postboten der Hund?
    (Is it the postman that the dog barks at?)
4. Subject - Object - Verb (SOV)

Examples:

  • Der Hund den Postboten bellt.
    (The dog barks at the postman.)

- In addition to these basic variations, there are other ways to modify sentence structure in German, such as using subclauses, relative clauses, and passive voice.

5. Subordinate clauses

- These are clauses that are dependent on the main clause and provide additional information. They can be introduced by conjunctions such as "weil" (because), "obwohl" (although), or "dass" (that).

Examples:

  • Ich spiele Tennis, weil es mir Spaß macht.
    (I play tennis because it's fun for me.)
6. Passive voice

- In the passive voice, the subject of the sentence receives the action rather than performing it. The passive is formed using the auxiliary verb "werden" and the past participle of the main verb.

Examples:

  • Das Buch wird von meinem Bruder gelesen.
    (The book is being read by my brother.)

- Understanding Satzstruktur is important for learners of German as it allows for more nuanced expression and effective communication.

Steigerung Superlativ Komparativ

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "Steigerung" is the German term for comparison, which means that German grammar has rules for comparing different forms of adjectives and adverbs.

- In German, there are two types of comparison: comparative and superlative.

2. Usage

1. Komparativ (Comparative)

- The comparative form is used to compare two things or people.

- In German, most adjectives are compared using the suffix "-er" (for example, "schneller" for "faster"):

Examples:

  • schneller (faster)

- If the adjective ends in "-d", "-t", "-s", "-ß", "-sch", "-x" or "-z", then the suffix "-er" is added after an "e":

Examples:

  • höher (higher)
  • leiser (quieter)

- When comparing adjectives with two or more syllables, the comparative is formed by adding "mehr" (meaning "more") before the adjective:

Examples:

  • mehr interessant (more interesting)

- Some adjectives have an irregular comparative form:

Examples:

  • gut → besser (better)
2. Superlativ (Superlative)

- The superlative form is used to compare three or more things or people.

- In German, most adjectives are compared using the suffix "-st" :

Examples:

  • schnellst (fastest)

- If the adjective ends in "-d", "-t", "-s", "-ß", "-sch", "-x" or "-z", then the suffix "-st" is added after an "e":

Examples:

  • höchst (highest)
  • leisest (quietest)

- When comparing adjectives with two or more syllables, the comparative is formed by adding "am meisten" (meaning "the most") before the adjective:

Examples:

  • am meisten interessant (most interesting)

- Some adjectives have an irregular superlative form:

Examples:

  • gut → am besten (the best)

- It's important to note that some adjectives have both regular and irregular forms for comparative and superlative. It's important to memorize these irregular forms.

Examples:

  • Schnell (fast)
    → Komparativ: schneller (faster)
    → Superlative: am schnellsten (fastest)
  • Groß (big) 
    → Komparativ: größer (bigger)
    → Superlative: am größten (biggest)
  • Gut (good) 
    → Komparativ: besser (better)
    → Superlative: am besten (the best)

Subjektive Bedeutung von Modalverben

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- The subjective meaning of modal verbs in German refers to how these verbs express the speaker's attitude or perspective towards the action or situation being described.

- In general, modal verbs are used to indicate possibility, necessity, ability, or permission, but their subjective meaning can vary depending on the context and the speaker's intentions.

2. Usage

- Here is a detailed explanation of the subjective meaning of modal verbs in German:

1. Modal verbs expressing possibility
a. können (to be able to, can)

- Can express either a factual or a hypothetical possibility, depending on the context.

Examples:

  • factual possibility:
    Ich kann heute nicht kommen.
    (I cannot come today.)
  • hypothetical possibility:
    Ich könnte heute kommen.
    (I could come today.)
b. mögen (to like, may)

- Expresses a polite request or a tentative possibility.

Examples:

  • polite request:
    Möchtest du bitte das Fenster schließen?
    (Would you please close the window?)
  • tentative possibility:
    Das könnte eine gute Idee sein.
    (That could be a good idea.)
c. dürfen (to be allowed to, may)

- Expresses permission or prohibition.

Examples:

  • permission:
    Du darfst das Buch behalten.
    (You may keep the book.)
  • prohibition:
    Du darfst hier nicht rauchen.
    (You are not allowed to smoke here.)
2. Modal verbs expressing necessity
a. müssen (to have to, must)

- Expresses a strong obligation or necessity.

Examples:

  • strong obligation:
    Ich muss heute arbeiten.
    (I have to work today.)
  • strong necessity:
    Du musst mehr Sport treiben.
    (You need to do more exercise.) 
b. sollen (to should, ought to)

- Expresses a recommendation, advice or expectation.

Examples:

  • recommendation:
    Du solltest früher ins Bett gehen.
    (You should go to bed earlier.)
  • expectation:
    Wir sollen morgen früh aufstehen.
    (We are expected to get up early tomorrow.)
c. brauchen (to need)

- Expresses a necessity or requirement.

Examples:

  • necessity:
    Ich brauche mehr Zeit für meine Arbeit.
    (I need more time for my work.)
  • requirement:
    Wir brauchen einen größeren Raum für die Veranstaltung.
    (We require a bigger room for the event.)
3. Modal verbs expressing ability
a. können (to be able to, can)

- Expresses ability or capability.

Examples:

  • ability:
    Ich kann gut schwimmen.
    (I can swim well.)
  • capability:
    Er kann fließend Deutsch sprechen.
    (He can speak German fluently.)
b. dürfen (to be allowed to, may)

- Expresses permission or ability.

Examples:

  • permission:
    Ich darf die Torte mitnehmen.
    (I am allowed to take the cake.)
  • ability:
    Sie darf alleine Auto fahren.
    (She is able to drive a car alone.)
4. Modal verbs expressing permission
a. dürfen (to be allowed to, may)

- Expresses permission or prohibition.

Examples:

  • permission:
    Darf ich bitte das Fenster öffnen?
    (May I please open the window?)
  • prohibition:
    Sie dürfen hier nicht parken.
    (You are not allowed to park here.)
b. lassen (to let, allow)

- Expresses permission or authorization.

Examples:

  • permission:
    Lass mich bitte das Buch lesen.
    (Let me read the book please.)
  • authorization:
    Der Chef hat ihn den Bericht unterschreiben lassen.

Trennbare Nicht Trennbare Verben

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- In German grammar, there are two types of verbs based on whether the prefix of the verb can be separated from the stem or not. These two types are known as trennbare Verben (separable verbs) and untrennbare Verben (inseparable verbs).

2. Usage

1. Trennbare Verben (Separable verbs)

- These are verbs in which the prefix can be separated from the stem and placed at the end of the sentence or clause.

- The prefix is usually stressed when it is separated from the stem.

- The infinitive form of these verbs is written as one word, but when conjugated, the prefix is separated from the stem and placed at the end of the sentence.

Examples:

  • aufstehen (to get up):
    → Ich stehe um 6 Uhr auf.
    (I get up at 6 o'clock.)
  • aussehen (to look like):
    → Sie sieht gut aus.
    (She looks good.)
  • anfangen (to begin):
    → Wir fangen um 9 Uhr an.
    (We begin at 9 o'clock.)
2. Untrennbare Verben (Inseparable verbs)

- These are verbs in which the prefix cannot be separated from the stem. The infinitive form of these verbs is also written as one word and when conjugated, the prefix remains attached to the stem.

Examples:

  • verstehen (to understand):
    → Ich verstehe die Frage nicht.
    (I don't understand the question.)
  • bekommen (to receive):
    → Er bekommt ein Geschenk.
    (He receives a present.)
  • vergessen (to forget):
    → Sie vergisst oft ihren Schlüssel.
    (She often forgets her key.)

- It is important to note that some verbs can be both separable and inseparable depending on the context of the sentence. In these cases, the meaning of the verb may change based on whether the prefix is separated or not.

Examples:

  • stellen (to place/set):
    -> [separable]: Ich stelle das Buch auf den Tisch.
    (I place the book on the table.)
  • verstehen (to comprehend):
    → [inseparable]: Ich verstehe den Text nicht.
    (I don't comprehend the text.)

Verben mit Präpositionen

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- Verbs with prepositions (Verben mit Präpositionen) are a common feature in German grammar. They are verbs that require a specific preposition to be used with their object in order to convey a particular meaning. These prepositions can be either accusative or dative, and the use of the preposition often changes the meaning of the verb.

Some common examples of verbs with prepositions include:

  • sich freuen auf (to look forward to)
  • warten auf (to wait for)
  • sich kümmern um (to take care of)
  • sich interessieren für (to be interested in)
  • sprechen über (to talk about)
  • denken an (to think about)

2. Usage

- When using verbs with prepositions, it is important to remember the correct order of the sentence. The preposition always comes after the verb and is followed by the object.

Examples:

  • Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
    (I am looking forward to the weekend.)
  • Wir warten auf den Zug.
    (We are waiting for the train.)
  • Er kümmert sich um seine kranke Mutter.
    (He is taking care of his sick mother.)
  • Ich interessiere mich für Kunst.
    (I am interested in art.)
  • Wir sprechen über das Wetter.
    (We are talking about the weather.)
  • Sie denkt an ihren Bruder.
    (She is thinking about her brother.)

- Verbs with prepositions can also have separable prefixes, which change the meaning of the verb and are separated from the verb when conjugated. For example:

Examples:

  • einladen zu
    (to invite to)
  • aussteigen aus
    (to get off of)

In these cases, the prefix goes to the end of the sentence, and the preposition and object remain in their usual positions.

Examples:

  • Ich lade dich zum Essen ein.
    (I invite you to dinner.)
  • Wir steigen aus dem Zug aus.
    (We get off the train.)

- Overall, understanding and correctly using verbs with prepositions is an important aspect of mastering German grammar.

Modal Verbs in German Grammar

Table Of Contents:

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage
  3. Conjugation of German Modal Verbs

1. Introduction

- The modal verbs in German are dürfen (be allowed to/may), können (be able to/can), mögen (to like/may), müssen (to have to/must), sollen (to ought to/should) and wollen (to want to). Modal verbs express ability, necessity, obligation, permission or possibility.

Examples:

  • Max will Automechaniker werden. Dafür muss er viel über Autos wissen. Sein Vater soll ihm alles erklären. In der Werkstatt darf Max seinem Vater helfen. Max kann sogar schon Reifen wechseln.

2. Usage

- We generally use modal verbs with the infinitive of the full verb. The meaning of the sentence changes depending on which modal verb we use.

Examples:

  • Max will/darf/soll Automechaniker werden.

- If the full verb is assumed to be obvious from context, we often leave it off in colloquial speech.

Examples:

  • Kannst du Deutsch (sprechen)?
  • Willst du eine Pizza (essen)?
  • Ich darf das (machen).

3. Conjugation of German Modal Verbs

- To conjugate modal verbs in the present and simple past, we use the finite form of the modal verb. However, to conjugate modal verbs in the perfect tense, we use the infinitive form of the modal verb and full verb and the finite form the auxiliary verb.

- We only use the past participle of a modal verb in the present perfect and past perfect tenses in sentences without a full verb.

Examples:

Trennbare Nicht Trennbare Verben

  1. Introduction
  2. Usage

1. Introduction

- "-los" and "-frei" are suffixes in German that are used to indicate the absence or lack of something. While they can be used interchangeably in some contexts, they have slightly different meanings and usages.

2. Usage

- There are some rules to follow when using these suffixes:

1. -los

- The suffix "-los" indicates a complete absence or lack of something. It is often used to describe a state of being without something:

Examples:

  • arbeitlos (unemployed)
  • machtlos (powerless)
  • sorglos (carefree)
  •  zahnlos (toothless)
  • kabellos (wireless)

- "-los" is used with nouns or verbs, It can also be added to verbs to indicate that the action is being performed without a specific object:

Examples:

  • schlaflos (sleepless)
  • planlos (without a plan)
2. -frei

- The suffix "-frei" indicates freedom or liberation from something. It is often used to describe a state of being without something negative:

Examples:

  • schmerzfrei (pain-free)
  • rauchfrei (smoke-free)
  • zuckerfrei (sugar-free)

- "-frei" is used mainly with nouns."-frei" can also be added to nouns to indicate that the product or service is free from a certain substance or ingredient:

Examples:

  • glutenfrei (gluten-free)
  • tierversuchsfrei (cruelty-free)

- There are some words where both "-los" and "-frei" can be used interchangeably.

Examples:

  • kostenlos (free of charge)
  • kostefrei (free of charge)

- While "-los" and "-frei" can sometimes be used interchangeably, they often have slightly different connotations.

Examples:

  • arbeitslos (unemployed)
    -> indicates a complete lack of work
  • arbeitsfrei (off work)
    → indicates a freedom from work
  • sorgenfrei (carefree)
    -> suggests a complete absence of worries
  • sorglos (carefree)
    → suggests a freedom from worries
  • geruchlos (odorless)
    → means that there is no smell
  • geruchsfrei (odorless)
    → means that there are no odors at all

- In summary, "-los" and "-frei" are suffixes in German that indicate the absence or lack of something and freedom or liberation from something, respectively. While they can be used interchangeably in some contexts, they often have slightly different connotations and are used to convey different shades of meaning. The choice between "-los" and "-frei" depends on the intended meaning and the word being used.
